item.title: PCT’s Northern Terminus Reopens, to Thru-Hikers’ Delight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.08
Monument 78 and the Canada/ US border marks the northern end of the Pacific Crest Trail (Photo: eppicphotography via Getty Images) The northern terminus of the Pacific Crest Trail is accessible again following a weekslong closure that foiled the plans of many northbound (NOBO) thru-hikers. The 50-mile stretch from Hart’s Pass to the Canadian border reopened on September 9 after having been officially closed since July 31 due to the Ptarmigan fire. Since then, finishing northbound thru-hikers have commemorated the finish line in a number of ways: In late July, some built a makeshift monument at the trailhead for Rainy Pass, just south of the closure. Others rerouted to the west, converging on a little-known obelisk at the Canadian border in the Mount Baker Wilderness. As of today, NOBO hikers still on the trail will be able to take the standard route to the border. “We’re overjoyed to know that the PCT up to the Northern Terminus is open again, as it is such an iconic and symbolic portion of the trail,” says Chris Rylee, Director of Marketing and Communication for the Pacific Crest Trail Association. “Appreciation and gratitude goes out to the Methow Valley Ranger District of Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest and all of the other partners, responders, and firefighters who coordinated massive efforts to keep PCT hikers and communities safe.” As thru-hiking season winds down on the PCT, the reopening comes at a difficult time for many hikers who recently left the trail. Last year, the average finish date for NOBO thru-hikers on the PCT was September 12, according to a survey by Halfway Anywhere. “For me it’s tough because all last month I’ve heard that there’s no possible chance they’d open to the terminus, despite the Ptarmigan fire being more and more contained. Because of this I changed my plans to skip that section and go east to the other monument,” says Reed “Steezy” Patricelli, a thru-hiker from Portland, Oregon who reached the Canadian border on September 6, just three days before the terminus reopened. “As much as it’s a bit annoying, to me its also not a huge deal,” he adds. On his reroute to monument 90, a spot on the Canadian border east of the official terminus, Patricelli says he spotted three black bears and 12 mountain goats: “I firmly believe that the trail is a different journey for everyone, and if the end of my journey had to be a different terminus, so be it!” For others still in the final stretch, the reopening means they’ll be able to cross the trail in the way they’d always imagined. Nicola “Sunflower” Whitbread, a NOBOer from England, is one of those hikers. Whitbread was on the trail in northern Oregon when she heard from another hiker that the terminus had reopened. “The PCT for me has always been about the journey and not the destination, but I won’t lie, I’m stoked that I’ll have the finish I’ve dreamed of for a decade.” In an Instagram post, the PCTA noted that lands east and west of the trail remain closed due to ongoing firefighting operations.

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape”: Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.84
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from an order by the BLM this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in the first place in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to re-categorize the definition of livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said that removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species away from its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led to the cancellation of American Prairies public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: Aspen Season Starts Now. See Peak Color On These 5 Trails
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.36
Fall foliage in Minnesota (Photo: Tammi Mild via Getty) For just a few precious weeks each year, the aspen forests of the West and Midwest flare into a golden wonderland. The trees flush from electric green to crayon-yellow, a color so vivid you could easily mistake the leaves for sunflower petals. River corridors become veins of ore. Mountainsides glow. Trails turn into vibrant tunnels carpeted in fallen gold. At high altitudes and latitudes, the color quickly blazes and fades. The narrow leaf-peeping window adds to the allure, but it also makes peak season easy to miss—especially if you don’t know where to go. These five trails are true autumn hot spots. Most wind through spectacular aspen groves, and a few offer sweeping vistas of golden forests far below. They make perfect places to hike this month and experience the spectacle of fall. If you let King Midas touch a forest, it might look something like this. While the nearby Maroon Bells are famed for their fall scenery, you’ll get a less crowded look at the golden goodness on the nearby Capitol Creek Trail. Target mid-September and hike 6 miles through dense aspen forest to the alpine lake beneath 14,137-foot Capitol Peak. Camp in one of the meadow’s secluded primitive sites to make a weekend of it, or return via the Capitol Peak Trail for a 12-mile lollipop loop. Capitol Creek Trail: Come mid-September, Wisconsin’s scattered aspens begin their fall transformation. For your best shot at concentrated color, head to Northern Highland-American Legion State Forest (NHAL), where a mix of wild and cultivated aspen groves keep the saturation dial turned all the way up. Our top picks: the Fallison Lake Trail, a 2.4-mile loop that wanders through glades and wetlands, and the Escanaba Loop, an 8.9-mile trek that winds past more than a dozen lakes and ponds. Whichever you choose, keep your eyes peeled for wildlife. Bald eagles and osprey soar over both trails, and beavers frequent the tree-fringed ponds. Fallison Lake Trail: Escanaba Loop: When fall starts in Michigan, the Porkies are one of the first places the tide of color touches. Aspens deepen their yellows around mid-September just as the forest’s famed hardwoods begin to blush orange and crimson. Lake of the Clouds is a local classic for color, but there’s no reason to stop at the parking-lot overlook; connect the North Mirror Lake and North Country National Scenic Trails for 13.2 miles and three summits over 1,500 feet. For regular foliage updates, check out West Michigan’s weekly fall color report. Lake of the Clouds Loop: Pando, a grove of interconnected clonal aspen trees, is widely considered to be one of the world’s largest single organisms. Its 47,000 genetically identical stems all share a single, interconnected root system. Most of the year, Pando blends into the surrounding foliage of Fishlake National Forest. But in late September, it goes up in a blaze of gold. To see it, park or camp at Doctor Creek Campground and wander the tangle of Forest Service roads southwest of the lake. For a longer trek, tackle the 16.4-mile Fishlake Loop, which offers nonstop views of the forest mirrored in the glassy water. Fishlake Loop: In the far north of the U.S., fall comes early. Take advantage by planning a mid- to late-September trip to the Boundary Waters, where lakeside vantage points unfurl expansive views of golden aspen forest. For top color, start at the Caribou Rock and Mossy Lake trailhead near the Canadian border. Tighten your laces and head north for a 13-mile linkup of Duncan, Rose, Patridge, Birch, and Moss Lakes. Be sure to leave enough time to linger on the cliffs overlooking Rose. When the timing’s right, the northern slopes turn into a riot of yellow, red, and peach. Rose and Duncan Lakes Loop: The hardest part of planning a fall foliage trip is hitting the colors as they’re peaking. Many factors affect how and when aspens (and other deciduous plants) turn color and shed their leaves. If you don’t time your hike right, you might arrive just before or after the colorful climax. There are tools that can help you, though. Check out Explore Fall’s interactive fall foliage map or the Farmer’s Almanac fall foliage map and leaf forecast. Both resources make it easy to time the best leaf-peeping experience.

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.67
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Why visitors to Prague should drink in a 'hospoda'
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.00
Why visitors to Prague should drink in a traditional pub Prague is synonymous with pubs – but for the real thing, travellers should venture away from its touristy centre and seek out an old-school "hospoda". My wife and I were sipping beers at a pub in Prague's Žižkov district when the bartender plopped two foamy pints of pilsner in front of us. We hadn't ordered them. We weren't even finished with the ones we were drinking. "Oh, we're in one of these pubs" I said, quickly covering my pint with a cardboard coaster. "When you've had enough, just do this." Most visitors to Prague are likely to linger in its Old Town Square, marvelling at its Gothic and Baroque splendour. They'll zigzag through the narrow cobblestone streets to the 14th-Century Charles Bridge and then trudge up to Prague Castle. Everyone should do this on a visit to Prague. But if you only explore its tourist-mobbed centre, as many people do, you'll miss out on one of the most quintessentially Czech cultural experiences: whiling away a few hours in a real Czech pub, where the beer only stops coming if you know the code. A city synonymous with beer It's no secret that Czechs love beer. After all, they drink nearly 150 litres of it per capita every year, making the Czech Republic the top beer-consuming nation in the world. Prague itself boasts the most pubs per person of anywhere on the planet. Your local expert David Farley is a food and travel writer who lived in Prague for three years and regularly writes articles for the BBC, The New York Times, The Guardian and other publications. He has probably spent a year or two of his life in Czech pubs. But just as most New Yorkers don't dine in Times Square and most Londoners don't eat in Piccadilly Circus, you'll rarely find Praguers drinking in Old Town, where bars cater largely to outsiders. Instead, to really get under the skin of Czech culture, you should venture to one of Prague's most atmospheric areas: Žižkov (pronounced Zheezh-kof), a gritty, working-class neighbourhood that has long had a proud reputation for its salt-of-the-earth pubs, and where the bartender's job is to make sure your glass is never empty. Home to hilly cobblestone streets and graffiti-tagged 19th-Century blocks of flats, Žižkov is home to classic pubs such as U Vystřelenýho Oka and U Slovanské Lípy. Despite its relative proximity to the centre of town – tram number 9 will get you there in about 20 minutes – you won't find a lot of guidebook-clutching tourists wandering around. "If you want to understand Czech pub culture, it's hard to find a better place than Žižkov," said Martin Havlin, co-founder of Prague Craft Beer Tours and a born-and-bred Žižkov denizen. "The big difference is that pubs in Žižkov are still mainly for locals. Nobody is trying too hard to look 'authentically Czech' for tourists. You'll find people having a beer after work, old guys at the same table they've probably occupied for 30 years, and a tapster who already knows what half the room is drinking." Žižkov's traditional Czech pubs, called hospoda, are one of the few places where people from all walks of Czech society mix naturally. Hospoda etiquette • If you you're sitting at a table, you're expected to wait for the server to take your order. Unless it's clearly indicated otherwise, don't order at the bar yourself. • Glasses are served wet at a hospoda, so always take the beer mat. It goes under your beer and will save you a wet table – and probably a few looks from the staff. • In Czech lager, foam is part of the beer, not something stealing space in the mug, so don't send it back because you think the glass hasn't been filled to the line. It has. "You can have a construction worker, lawyer, university professor and pensioner sitting at neighbouring tables drinking exactly the same beer," said Jakub Neužil, Havlin's colleague at Prague Craft Beer Tours. "Most importantly, though, they would understand that going to the pub in Czech culture isn't necessarily about 'going out drinking'. Historically, the hospoda has been an extension of the living room: somewhere to meet friends, discuss football, politics, work and life. Beer happens to be at the centre of it." These "living rooms" are great places for travellers to meet English-speaking regulars. A simple "how long have you been coming here?" may soon lead to stories about how hospoda have played an instrumental role in Czech history. Prague was the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and until World War Two, German was widely spoken here alongside Czech. By the latter half of the 19th Century, Czech speakers had begun separating themselves from the German population, and the Czech National Revival, which would eventually result in the creation of Czechoslovakia in 1919, was fomented in Czech cafes and pubs. "At the time, pubs played an important role as gathering places for revivalists, patriots, politicians, writers, artists et cetera; they became centres of associational and cultural life and were one of the few places where Czech was commonly spoken," said Dr Jiří Vinopal, a Senior Fellow at the Institute of Sociology at the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. During the heavily oppressive socialist period from 1948 to 1989, Vinopal explains that Czech pubs were "used more as an environment for escape". More like this: Today, pubs are as much a part of Czech life as ever – and a big draw for tourists – but it's increasingly harder to find the kind of old-fashioned hospoda where historical conversations flow as easily as the beer. The city's modern offerings tend to be cleaner and smoke free, with classic fried cheese sharing menu space with dishes like pumpkin soup and cauliflower pancakes. How to drink at a real Czech pub? Havlin's advice is to simply find a busy pub in Žižkov, sit down, order a beer and don't rush. "Watch how people behave, how the beer is poured, order some Czech pub food and maybe start a conversation – and definitely don't leave after one beer." He adds, "That’s the beauty of a real [hospoda]. You're not being shown Czech culture – you're just sitting in the middle of it. And after the second or third beer, you might even start feeling like a local." While sipping your beer and meeting regulars, you may also notice the way Czech bartenders treat Czech beer differently than the more touristy pubs in Prague's historical centre. It starts with the bartender taking a chilled mug and re-rinsing it using a counter-top spray device to ensure there's no fat residue. Then they use the Czech-invented Lukr side-tap to pour the beer, ensuring there's at least three fingers' worth of foam; the side-tap allows the bartender more control of the foam and emits far less gas into the drink than the traditional top pull, making the beer from the Lukr side tap less likely to bloat the stomach. "This developed because beer has been such an important part of Czech culture," said Lucie Janečkova, co-founder of Institut PIVO, a Prague-based school providing beer-focused bartender training. "We've learned that brewing a good beer is only half of the job. What happens to it between the brewery and the guest can completely change the final experience." There is a common saying among Czech bartenders: 'The brewer brews the beer; the bartender makes it.'" There's also an etiquette to drinking once your beer arrives. "When you get a beautifully poured beer, drink it while it's fresh – don't leave it sitting on the table for half an hour," added Janečkova. "And if you're drinking with others, clink glasses with your first beer and say 'cheers' in Czech – 'na zdraví!'" She adds, "And perhaps the most Czech rule of all: if someone says, 'Let's go for one beer,' you probably shouldn't make any plans for the rest of the evening." And, as my wife learned, if you're in a pub in Žižkov, even the bartender won't let you go until you finally put that beer mat atop your empty mug. --

item.title: Magical Midnight Margarita
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.36
Fans of the cult classic film Practical Magic may recognize some version of this cocktail. The “Midnight Margarita” is inspired by a scene in which two characters blend up a witchy brew to the soundtrack of Harry Nilsson’s “Coconut.” Some fans even start the movie at exactly 11:12 p.m., so the pivotal moment arrives at the stroke of midnight. While the movie’s cocktail appears to be a standard standard frozen margarita—no eye of newt or toe of frog, (maybe hair of the dog if you prefer tequila and lime in the morning)—but our version leans into the magic. Blackberries give the drink its deep purple color, while coconut water adds a subtle sweetness and makes the frozen version especially refreshing. Serve it on the rocks or blended. If serving on the rocks, garnish with a torched rosemary sprig for a smoky, spellbinding flourish. More tequila drinks to cheers to at midnight: Paloma; Citrus Slushy; Aperol-Kombucha Cocktail How to make a frozen version: Because freezing can dull flavors, adding a little extra lime juice perks this version up. We’ve also increased the coconut water so you won’t have to dilute the drink with plain ice. | Yield: Makes 1 | Total time: 10 minutes plus chilling | Ingredients - 1 cup coconut water - Flaky sea salt - 3 limes - 5 blackberries - 2 oz. tequila blanco - 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec) - ½ tsp. sugar Method - Pour 1 cup coconut water into an ice cube tray. Freeze until solid, at least 2 hours or, ideally, 12 hours. - Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 3 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 3 oz). - Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. - Blend coconut water ice cubes, 2½ oz. lime juice, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a blender until smooth. Pour into glass with blackberries. (Save any remaining lime juice in an airtight container in the fridge up to 3 days.) Recipe information - Total Time 10 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Ingredients 2 5 2 2 1 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 2 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 2 oz). Step 2Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. Step 3Combine lime juice, 2 oz. coconut water, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or Triple Sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a cocktail shaker filled with ice. Cover and shake until outside of shaker is very cold, about 30 seconds. Step 4Fill glass with blackberries with ice cubes. Strain cocktail over and garnish with a rosemary sprig, briefly singed over a flame, if desired.

item.title: Blueberry Protein Pancakes (No Protein Powder)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.11
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Tofu in blueberry pancakes?! Your eyes do not deceive you. Here, silken tofu acts as a binding agent in these protein-packed vegan blueberry pancakes. As there are no eggs in this recipe, you’ll need as much help with leavening as possible to cut through the density of the tofu. This means adding both baking powder and soda—and a lot of it. Baking powder (make sure to use the aluminum-free kind to mitigate any unpleasant flavor) will activate with the water and again when the batter hits the heat; baking soda will react with the water and the acid in the brown sugar. The result is a fluffy, crisp-edged pancake with a slightly chewy, almost mochi-like interior. Small wild blueberries are best, but whatever kind you find at the store will work. As is the case with most baked goods—even those that technically don’t go into the oven—these pancakes are most successful when the ingredients are measured by weight with a scale. If measuring by volume with measuring cups, it can be easy to pack in a little extra flour. If so, you may need to add about a tablespoon or so more water; you want the batter to be the approximate consistency of pourable whole-milk yogurt (not thick Greek-style). Discover more Good for You recipes here: Veggie Club Sandwich; Berry Protein Smoothie; Chopped Salad With Sardines and Preserved Lemon Read More: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 15 minutes - Yield Makes about 16 Ingredients 1½ ½ 3 2 1 1 1 5 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 1½ cups (188 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (62 g) whole wheat flour, 3 Tbsp. light brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. aluminum-free baking powder, 1 tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Step 2Blend tofu and liquid from one 16–17-oz. package silken tofu in a blender until very smooth. Scrape down sides and add 1 Tbsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil and 1½ cups water; blend until mixture is very smooth. Scrape into bowl with dry ingredients and gently fold in with a whisk. Step 3Heat a dry large nonstick skillet over medium for 3 minutes. Drizzle in 1½ tsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil. Pour 2 scant ⅓-cupfuls of batter into skillet, leaving space around each. Top each pancake with about 1½ tsp. fresh or frozen wild blueberries. Cook pancakes until tops start to look matte, about 4 minutes. Gently flip and cook until golden underneath, about 4 minutes. Transfer pancakes to a plate or wire rack. (Alternatively, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in a 300° oven while you make the rest). Working in 7 more batches, repeat process with remaining oil, batter, and blueberries, adjusting heat as needed to keep pancakes from absorbing too much oil or burning. Step 4Serve pancakes with pure maple syrup. Do Ahead: Pancakes can be made 3 months ahead. Let cool, then stack between sheets of parchment paper and place in an airtight container or resealable plastic bag and freeze. Reheat in a toaster or toaster oven until warmed through.

item.title: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.89
These lettuce wraps with spicy crumbled chicken, fresh herbs, and lime are a longtime favorite of Bon Appétit readers (and staff). Inspired by larb, the saucy filling gets its savory-sweet heat from a blend of soy sauce, fish sauce, brown sugar, and sriracha, with plenty of garlic and scallions. The combination of warm, spicy ground chicken, cool, crisp lettuce, fresh cilantro or mint, crunchy store-bought fried shallots, and bright citrus comes together in just about 20 minutes. It’s a high-reward dinner for very little effort. Chicken lettuce wraps FAQ What kind of lettuce should I use? Bibb lettuce is our first choice: Its leaves are tender and pliable enough to fold around the spicy chicken filling without tearing. Boston and butter lettuce are good substitutes, while romaine “boats” will give the wraps more crunch. Can I make these lettuce wraps with a different ground meat? Absolutely. Ground pork, beef, turkey, or lamb can be swapped for the ground chicken without otherwise changing the recipe. For fattier meats, like ground beef and lamb, you can start with 1½ Tbsp. oil. What should I serve with chicken lettuce wraps? These lettuce wraps make a complete light dinner on their own, but steamed jasmine rice or coconut rice will make the meal more substantial. You can also skip the lettuce and spoon the chicken, herbs, fried shallots, and lime over rice for an easy rice bowl. Recipe information - Total Time 20 minutes - Yield 2 servings Ingredients 3 2 2 2 3 6 4 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Mix 3 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. light or dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. sriracha, and 2 tsp. fish sauce in a small bowl to combine; set aside. Step 2Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a skillet over medium. Add 6 scallions, thinly sliced, and 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened (a little color is okay), about 3 minutes. Add 1 lb. ground chicken and lightly season with kosher salt. Cook, breaking up meat with spoon and tossing occasionally, until cooked through, 5–7 minutes. Add reserved soy sauce mixture and cook, tossing occasionally, until liquid is reduced by half, about 2 minutes. Step 3Serve chicken mixture with Bibb lettuce leaves, mint leaves and/or cilantro leaves with tender stems, lime wedges, store-bought fried shallots, and more sriracha for making lettuce wraps. item.title: Listen to BA Bake Club's Podcast on Plum Karpatka (Polish Cream Puff Cake)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.63
For the past six years, senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewyczk has been trying to get a karpatka recipe published. Even though he’d never made one in its entirety before. But he knew BA’s Bake Club was the perfect place to showcase what he calls the drag queen of Polish desserts. “I’ve made every component before,” Jesse tells his cohost Shilpa Uskokovic. “I just haven’t arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion.” “We hope that that's what people in Bake Club take away,” Shilpa adds. “That by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they’re the first time you’re making them.” Jesse’s version has an American twist (a no-bake cheesecake filling) and a nod to his Polish roots (the plum compote). Listeners also weighed in with questions about and photos of their sky-high desserts, and we awarded our Baker of the Month. We also had a visit from a beloved star baker in The Great British Baking Show (a.k.a. Bake-Off for those in the UK). Season nine finalist Ruby Bhogal stopped by the podcast to talk about her new book Around the World in 80 Cakes. And yes, there is a karpatka in it! Find Ruby Bhogal @rubybhogal and on Substack. Shilpa Uskokovic: I'm Shilpa Uskokovic. Jesse Szewczyk: And I'm Jesse Szewczyk. SU: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit. JS: And this is BA Bake Club. SU: Bake Club is Bon Appétit's community of confident and curious bakers. JS: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet. SU: Every month, we publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know. JS: Then you'll go bake, and you can send us any questions you have or pictures of your finished creations. SU: And we get together here on the podcast to talk about the recipe. JS: The September Bake Club recipe for glazed apple pie fritters is live now on bonappetit.com, and we'll tell you a bit more about those at the end of the episode. SU: But today, today we're diving into Jesse's Polish roots with his recipe for a Plum Karpatka. JS: Listen, I've been pitching of Karpatka for years. SU: You have? JS: Okay, I'm going to be real. I didn't grow up eating Karpatka. And we'll explain to you what this is. I feel like I'm building suspense here. SU: Yes. JS: But it's this Polish cake that I stumbled across several years ago, and I was like, "This is cool." SU: How do you describe it in your text? I love the phrase that you use. JS: Oh, and they let me keep it. I called it the drag queen of Polish desserts because it's just big, boisterous, and kind of silly. SU: Showy. JS: Yeah. SU: It's a lovely dessert. JS: Thank you. SU: And you gave it a really nice ... In a way, it was almost like a very New York spin with a cheesecake. JS: Yeah, yeah, yeah. SU: That's the whole thing. Okay. The photos that our Bake Clubbers have sent in of the Karpatka have been absolutely incredible. JS: They're big. Yeah. SU: I feel like there were a lot of skills that came together in this one from past Bake Club bakes. JS: Yeah. Those of you who have been around for a while, we did a Paris-Brest, which is this big kind of tire of choux that you fill with a sweet filling. SU: And for those who are listening, it's choux, as in choux pastry. JS: Choux paste, yes. SU: Okay. Sorry, Jesse. Didn't mean to cut you off. JS: Not the gym shoes, a big tire of choux. And that was a traditional way to cook pâte à choux, you can make cream puffs, éclairs. And this is baking choux in a cake pan, which I feel like is a very unique way to bake it. So, it's like building upon that foundation we learned several months back to create something completely different. SU: I love that you did that, because that's what baking is about. It's like these few things that you have, and then you re-spin it in different directions. Okay. Before we go any further, let's take a moment to get a brief step-by-step tour of this recipe. Okay? And for that, we're going to need our jaunty Bake Club music. Here it is. Okay. Jesse, walk us through this recipe. JS: Yeah, and buckle up because it's a challenge. Not hard, but it takes some effort. Okay, let's start. SU: Sure. JS: So, you're first going to start by making plum compote, and that's very easy. You just cook some plums with sugar and salt. And then when that's nice and thick, you're just going to finish it with some lemon zest juice and some vanilla, and that's your jam. So, make sure you cool that though, because it'd be warm, you need it to be nice and cool and thick. So, as that's cooling, you're going to make your pâte à choux, which we might be familiar with. So, you're going to bring a stick of butter, cut into little pieces, some sugar, some salt, and water to a simmer. And with simmering, you're going to add some flour, and then cook that into this thick doughy paste, and then take that out, let it cool for a while, and then you're going to whip that in a mixer with some eggs. Divide that between two cake bands and bake them, and then watch as they dramatically turn into these giant wonky discs. So, cool your discs, and as those are cooling, you can work on your filling. So, this is like a no-bake cheesecake. So, you're going to start by blooming some gelatin in some cold water, let that sit, then heat up just a tiny bit of cream, pour that over that, so it dissolves the gelatin. And then, to that, you're going to add some cream cheese, some powdered sugar, some vanilla, some salt, and then you're going to beat that all together while adding some more heavy cream to kind of lighten it. And then that's your filling. So, you can assemble everything at this point. So, those two choux puff discs you have, you keep one in a cake pan, and then you put your filling in, you swirl it with the jam, put the other on top like a sandwich, let it sit overnight, and it sets into this beautiful Karpatka. And that's that. SU: The drag queen of Polish desserts. JS: The drag queen, that's how the drag queen gets her beat on, the full beat. SU: Have you ever made Karpatka before this? JS: I'm being called out, and the answer is honestly no. SU: I love that. JS: So, this was a learning experience for us all. SU: Yes. JS: Yeah, and it was really fun. SU: I want to get philosophical here and be like, just because we've never made something before doesn't mean we don't have the authority to make it. Do you know? JS: Well, I've made every component. SU: Exactly. JS: I just haven't arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion. SU: Exactly. JS: Yes. SU: And we hope that that's what people in Bake Club, our members, take away, that by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they're the first time you're making them. JS: Shilpa, that's beautiful. SU: Thank you. Okay. What occasion do people ... Well, it's a cake. You can eat it at any time. But traditionally, I wonder when a Karpatka is usually served and eaten. JS: I think traditionally in Polish culture, it's for holidays, like Easter, Christmas, and I guess this was my summer version. The flirty summer version of a Karpatka. SU: And I think something, the Easter connection, I'm thinking about ... My husband is Serbian, and they do- JS: Yeah, my husband. SU: And they also have a lot of choux-based pastries, especially around- JS: Like what? SU: They have something called a Princes Krofne, which is éclairs. JS: Sure. SU: Actually, they're cream puffs, to be honest, but no chocolate top. I'm not sure why they call it Princes Krofne, but they are. But I think Easter and Christmas, especially Easter, I think it's after that fasting period, and then you're able to use all these rich ingredients like eggs, which the defining factor of choux, I think, is how many eggs there are in the pastry. JS: Yeah, it's like eggy. It's like doughy, eggy in a nice way, like custardy. SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. So, I want to talk more about the pâte à choux, because it is really deeply fascinating. But let's start with the first component that you named, which is the compote. Why did you decide to go with plums? JS: Well, a few reasons. I guess you can kind of use any jam you want. If you want cheap, you can buy a thing of jam, that's fine. But I was thinking, "Oh, what is a late summer produce?" Because it's not quite the peak of summer anymore, nor is it cold weather. And I feel like stone fruit is kind of that transitional fruit, but also plums are very traditional in Polish cuisine and baking. In American culture, we have all these sayings about apples, like, "An apple a day keeps the doctor away," or, "A good apple," or various things. The Polish equivalent is plums. There's all these different sayings about plums, and it's just ... And also, when you use red plums and you make a compote, that color is crazy saturated. SU: Yes, it's very dramatic. JS: It stains your hand saturated, and I thought that would just be stunning. And I don't know, stone fruit's so underrated. Yeah. So, I really wanted to give it a moment. SU: How chunky do you like your compote? JS: Nah. SU: Not at all? JS: A little bit. SU: Yeah. Does it matter for the Karpatka, how chunky it is? Can people leave it a bit chunkier, or make it a bit smoother? JS: They can leave it chunky, but just make sure you cook it down enough that it's not wet, because you want it to thicken up enough that it doesn't seep out. SU: So, you want to dry enough moisture, so when you slice it, it doesn't just weep all over. JS: Yeah. SU: It's thick and jammy. JS: So, if you're able to keep chunks while cooking it out, that's cool. SU: Sure. JS: But I think it might be hard. SU: Got it. JS: Yeah, yeah. SU: And plums are pretty high in pectin. JS: They are, yeah. SU: They make a good jam. JS: Yeah. When it's warm, it can feel a bit loose, but then after overnight in the fridge, it does thicken up quite a bit. Yeah. SU: Is that your recommended amount of chill time for the compote? Can anybody chill it for less and still manage to get away with it? JS: I think you could. If you chill it for an hour, and it's a shallow metal bowl, you're fine. Also, you can, if you're in a rush, which I was many times making this, I'll put it on a sheet tray, so it's a very thin layer, and then that chills in, I don't know, 20 minutes. SU: Smart. JS: Yeah. SU: So, you just don't want it to be so warm that it will melt like the cheesecake filling. That's all we're trying to do, really? JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. JS: Yeah, pretty much. SU: Okay. Okay, that's great. Okay. We'll move on to the second component, which is our star. JS: The choux. SU: The choux. I remember this is when you had a bit of a eureka moment. JS: Yeah. I mean, honestly, looking back, I'm like, maybe I'm stupid, but- SU: Stop. Don't say that about yourself. JS: Okay. I'm sorry. SU: Apologize to Jesse, my friend. JS: Okay, let's move on. So, okay. When you make choux, you bring your water to a simmer with your butter, and then, in that, you can add salt and sugar if you want, and then you add your flour, and you cook it in the pan till it kind of sticks. And then, that glob, you mix with eggs, and people mix it by hand. They just add the eggs. Sometimes they even crack the eggs right in the pan once it's cooled a bit. Some people do it in a mixer, and I thought that incorporating the eggs was just mixing them in. That's that. The first couple tests, it got some nice height, sure. It puffed so much. I'm like, "That's it." So, just you need to literally mix the shit out of your choux, and incorporate that air physically, mechanically, and it's going to expand and give you two times the puff. SU: Does it matter if you use a stand mixer versus a hand mixer? JS: I don't think so. I think the stand mixer probably works better in this case, but you could use both. SU: Yeah. The trick is to just keep going. JS: Just keep going. SU: With the crap out of it. JS: Yeah. So, you get a lot of air incorporated in there, which makes sense because it's egg-based. SU: Yeah, and the egg is trapping all that air. JS: Yeah. So, it was really fun though to watch it expand. I remember some, we'll get to this later, but someone was like, "Oh, because it expanded too much." I'm like, "No such thing." SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: And then how ... Because choux, in many ways, is a very unique sort of dough. You're really cooking, you're pre-cooking the flour into this weird, as you said, glob. JS: Yeah. SU: How do you know when it's ready to come off the heat? JS: Sure. For me, when I'm cooking this dough, when I see a very thin kind of ... SU: Because there's enough moisture, I guess, gone, so it starts sticking to the bottom. JS: Yeah. I think it's, at that point, the starches are pre-gelatinized and you're good to go. SU: Sure. JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. So, you make a choux, and you said one of the secrets to getting a really dramatic puff is to really beat it aggressively. JS: Yes. SU: Then you're putting it in the oven, and this you bake it in two cake pans. JS: Yes. SU: Which unlike your Paris-Brest, which you bake on a sheet tray. JS: Yeah, like freeform. I would suggest taking a little bit of your choux and making little blobs, and then use- SU: Goo dots. JS: Goo dots, and then gluing your parchment down, and then smearing the choux on top. SU: Got it. JS: And if it's not perfect, it's fine because I found, say, it's uneven, it kind of just adds to the uneven whimsy texture that you're going to get. So, you don't have to be too precious. SU: And what about greasing the sides of the pan? Do we have to- JS: No. SU: Got it. JS: Nope. SU: Not at all. JS: I learned that the hard way. It's kind of like a souffle, when it needs to climb on something, like the sugar. I think that greasing the sides made it too slippery, and it didn't want to expand upward. Yes. SU: Can we extend the same logic to the pan, if somebody uses a non-stick pan? JS: I would not recommend a non-stick cake pan here. I think it would ultimately be fine, but I think, for the best results, I would avoid. SU: Yeah, just use a regular aluminum pan. JS: Exactly. SU: The thing is we learn. JS: I know. A lot of strange nuance here. SU: Okay. Jesse, obviously, it wouldn't be a Bake Club recipe without a little twist, and this one comes in the form of one of my favorites. JS: Something we never use here. SU: Philadelphia, where are you at? JS: Yeah. It's not instant pudding this time. It's cream cheese. SU: It's cream cheese. Okay. Tell me how you ended up with cream cheese as your Karpatka filling. JS: Yes. So, this breaks away from traditional Karpatka construction. So, Karpatka, typically, is filled with something a bit less stable, like a creme mousseline, or a pastry cream that's lightened with whipped cream or stuff. And I started there. I did. And when we cut into it, it proved perhaps too ephemeral. It died quite quickly. It weeps. That's just kind of the nature of Karpatka. It is what it is. SU: I remember that each step, where it was like you made this whipped cream filling, and then you said, "Okay, let's use something stable." SU: While everything is still in the pan? JS: Yes. SU: Okay. JS: And then put your hand on top. SU: Okay. JS: And then confidently, in one swift motion, flip it out. SU: Got it. JS: And nothing's going to happen. It's going to be fine. SU: Got it. JS: And that's that, put powdered sugar on top, and it's done. SU: Okay, okay. So, you put a plate on top. JS: I just use my hand. SU: You do? JS: Yeah. It really- SU: You do it from your hand? You then transfer it onto a plate? JS: Yes. SU: Oh my God. I didn't know this. JS: Yeah. item.title: 3-Ingredient Curry Pumpkin Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.64
This dead simple, three-ingredient soup houses a wealth of flavor with a shockingly trim ingredient list. Made by sizzling curry paste in oil, then adding a can of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, this cozy soup is a celebration of simplicity, creating something that tastes far more complex than it was to make. For the best flavor, I like to use the Maesri brand curry paste, leaning on its warm intensity to lend the soup its depth, but the ubiquitous Thai Kitchen, sold in almost all grocery stores, is also nice, producing a gentle heat. It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Preparation - Transfer a couple of spoonfuls or so of one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, stirred well, to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Heat 1 Tbsp. unrefined coconut oil or other oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 2 Tbsp. red curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 2–3 minutes. Add one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, remaining coconut milk in can, and 1½ cups water. Increase heat to high and bring soup to a simmer. Remove pot from heat. Taste soup and season with kosher salt if needed. Ladle into bowls and drizzle some reserved coconut milk into each bowl.

item.title: Newport, Rhode Island, Is New England’s Gilded Jewel—Here’s Where to Eat, Stay, and Play
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.38
Newport, Rhode Island, has certainly been having a moment as of late. You can attribute it to the Gilded Age dramas taking over small screens, the old-money aesthetic taking over TikTok, the Real Housewives of Rhode Island taking over Bravo, or just the fact that it’s beyond beautiful all year long. Either way, it’s undeniable that this compact coastal city has become a mecca of sorts for travelers eager to live out their East Coast fantasies—seafood, seersucker, sailboats, and all. But truth be told, Newport has never been a bad idea. The charming city has been a popular summer destination since the early 19th century, first as a playground for America’s elite, with families like the Vanderbilts and Astors building massive mansions along the water to serve as vacation homes (more on those later). Today, it’s a little less exclusive and a hot spot year-round, with New Englanders and international visitors alike spending sunny days becoming one with the sand at Easton’s Beach, breezy afternoons hiking the Cliff Walk, and chilly nights imbibing their way through Bowen’s Wharf before retreating to shingled cottages and luxurious hotels across town. If all that sounds like your kind of bliss, keep reading for a guide to seeing Newport in all its glory, as compiled by two New Yorkers who have been returning over and over again for the past decade. Here’s where to eat, stay, and play in the City by the Sea. Where to eat We’d argue the food and drink scene in Newport is reason enough to come to town, boasting old favorites and newer hubs that have given the city’s dining scene some fresh energy. Early birds, hit up Cru Cafe for a cozy bistro vibe and elevated comfort dishes like smoked salmon avocado toast. If you’re willing to wait in line, The Nitro Bar is a newer favorite (especially among influencers) with coffee and pastries that just might be worth the hype. Or, head to locally loved Franklin Spa, a legendary diner that hasn't changed its retro greasy-spoon energy in decades, and still serves one of the best lunches in town. Speaking of lunch, if the weather calls for it, take yours alfresco. Use Bowen’s Wharf as your hub: Belly up at 22 Bowen’s outdoor bar-restaurant area, have a casual seafood lunch at The Mooring, or get your clam chowder fix at The Black Pearl, with its lively dockside setting. You'll also find Clarke Cooke House, one of Newport's most popular restaurants, at the wharf. Its ship-like setting is one for the books, and the bistro offers a big menu spanning summer sushi to burgers, native cod, and even steak frites. For something less serious, Wally’s Weiners is another classic, and the kind of place you'll want to work into a day of wandering around Thames Street, known for being the center of the city. For harbor views and a Mediterranean-inspired menu, head to Flora, one of the newer names in town housed within the Gardiner House hotel. White Horse Tavern, on the other hand, offers classic Americana, with upscale farm-to-table dining (and stellar rum drinks) inside a building dating back to 1673. Crossing the bridge into Jamestown? Head to Beech if you want dinner to be the main event, with tasty, seasonal American fare headed up by locals. Where to stay Newport has no shortage of gorgeous hotels scattered from busy Thames Street to breezy Castle Hill Cove. Most guest rooms fall on the smaller side—this is a compact city, after all—but the best properties go big on glamour, offering gobsmacking views, old-world interiors, and exceptional in-house eateries and wellness facilities. Those looking for a taste of the Gilded Age should opt for spots like The Vanderbilt, an Auberge property built by a member of the Vanderbilt family in 1908, or Francis Malbone House, a Georgian-style mansion that dates back to 1760. If you’re all about location, location, location, book The Chanler at Cliff Walk for easy access to the popular waterfront hiking trail, Hammetts Hotel if you want to be steps from some of the city’s best bars and restaurants, or Forty 1º North Hotel Marina Resort to be so close to the water you’re basically swimming. Whether you’re staying there or not, you don't skip a stop inside Castle Hill Inn, a landmark Victorian mansion and one of the most iconic hotels in town. With an incredible location atop rocky bluffs that overlook the sailboat-studded ocean, the property’s Lawn Terrace is where you’ll want to grab a glass of Sauv Blanc and pretend you’re an Astor. Of course, hotels in Newport can be pricey, so if you’re on a budget or traveling with a group, an Airbnb might be a better bet—especially if the sound of a kitchen or common hangout space tickles your fancy. You can find smaller homes and apartments in Newport proper, like this four-bedroom with harbor views right downtown or this minimalist waterfront condo in the Historic District, but many visitors look to Middletown, Rhode Island—a town right outside Newport—for bigger, more affordable rentals. This adorable three-bedroom cottage with a shingled façade, for example, is technically in Middletown, but just five minutes from downtown Newport. Where to play The soul of Newport is rooted in the very concept of play. It’s a family-friendly destination and a romantic coastal escape; a place where sweet boutiques meet cool bars and Gilded Age history meets a working harbor. In the warmer months, chase the sea: Easton’s Beach is the most convenient option near town, Gooseberry Beach is tucked along Ocean Drive, and Second (or Sachuest) Beach offers a long stretch of sand and Atlantic surf. Post up at Second for a lobster roll and fries (sold from a beachside concession stand, the best), then grab an icy, refreshing Del’s Lemonade served from its iconic truck before heading home. Oh, and before you go, buy your next beach read at Commonwealth Books of Newport in the Historic Hill neighborhood. If you time it right, you can hit Newport's renowned Jazz Festival and the Newport Folk Festival, both hosted annually at the end of July (and sometimes running through early August). Plan in advance to secure tickets, as they can go quickly. For a more last-minute excursion that's completely free to the public, walk the Cliff Walk on the southeastern shoreline. The scenic coastal path threads between the Atlantic and the Newport Mansions, which, of course, you'll want to go inside and tour. If you’d rather be on the water than beside it, Sail Newport offers a Try Sailing experience, as well as afternoon-to-sunset sails. For something further from the coast, the International Tennis Hall of Fame is a great rainy day pit stop for exploring the history of the beloved sport and sniffing your way through the gardens surrounding the iconic grass courts. The Preserve in Blackstone Valley offers guided horseback tours, carriage rides, and sunset strolls, while Shephard’s Run Winery is a dreamy estate that gives you an excuse to head inland in South Kingstown for a tasting. As for a great Irish pub, The Fastnet has frosty beers on tap, while O’Brien’s is ever-abuzz and makes a mean house mudslide. If you want to make a night of it, have a drink and bites at Hotel Viking’s French-inspired Pescadou restaurant, then dance to the live DJ at its rooftop bar, Cap Club. Midtown Oyster Bar is perfect for a nightcap.

item.title: Thousands of Flights Disrupted at UK Airports Due to Air Traffic Control Issue
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.73
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following an air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday, September 8. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue through Wednesday as airlines and airports work through backlogged flights. The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologized for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken “longer than hoped.” An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” London Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before traveling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before traveling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday, September 9 have already been canceled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by the disruption are repositioned. Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or canceled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 (approximately $300) per person to £520 (approximately $700) per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is canceled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Or, if your flight departs from an EU country and arrives in the UK (operated by either an EU or a non-EU airline). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. item.title: Boston’s Best Lobster Rolls Include a Secret Off-Menu Pick
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.88
New Englanders grow up on unfussy seafood like lobster rolls the way other people grow up on tacos or barbecue—foods so embedded in the way of life of a particular place that you don’t realize how special they are until you start traveling. Now, when I’m away from home, I find that lobster rolls are seen as an expensive delicacy. Yes, lobster rolls are special; they exist in the city’s glitzier and fine-dining restaurants, and their prices have skyrocketed in more recent years. But they’re also just as common at fast food counters in the suburbs and fishmonger docks up and down the coast. And just like paying $6 a gallon for gas on a California road trip, or $43 for a martini at Bemelman’s Bar in Manhattan, having a lobster roll in Boston is a worthwhile investment every once in a while. It's simply what you do when you’re here. That being said, not all lobster rolls are created equal—and many (sometimes controversial) variations exist. A purist will say that a proper one must—must!—be served on a split-top bun that’s been griddled until golden brown, while others make compelling arguments for fancy swaps like brioche rolls. Then there’s the lobster meat itself, served either as a simply dressed cold salad (Maine style) or warm and buttered (Connecticut style)—but that’s more of a personal preference. The good news? There are many, many lobster rolls to experience in Boston, ranging from textbook classics to more chef-driven interpretations. Here's where to find the best. Row 34 Chef Jeremy Sewall knows a thing or two about good fish, and his popular Row 34 restaurants (with locations in Fort Point and in Cambridge’s Kendall Square) are where you go for excellent beer, interesting wines, and a chef’s sensibility. Here, the lobster roll is surprisingly personal, with lobster sourced from chef Sewall’s cousin Mark, who captains a boat in York Harbor, Maine. There are two versions here: a warm buttered roll with steamed tail, claw and knuckle meat and tucked into a traditional split-top bun; and the other, the Ethel’s Creamy Lobster Roll, named for Sewall’s grandmother and folded together with celery, red onion, pickles, mayonnaise, crème fraîche, lemon, celery salt and black pepper. The cold, creamy one comes on a rosemary brioche bun that is griddled to order and is nothing short of heavenly. James Hook & Co. James Hook & Co. is the alpha and omega of Boston lobster rolls; a platonic ideal of what a lobster roll should be. The family-run seafood business operating on the Boston waterfront for over 100 years is an adorable, unassuming shack on shiny, transformed Atlantic Avenue downtown—this is where any good lobster roll tour of the city should begin (or end). The company ships over 50,000 pounds of lobster daily, both online and to wholesale distributors nationwide, so they know a thing or two about quality. The rolls here come in two sizes and two styles, either chilled or warm with butter. While you’re here, don’t overlook the other seafood specialties; the double-stuffed scallop, clam chowder, and lobster mac and cheese make for a perfect shared side. Saltie Girl If James Hook is the lobster roll in its natural habitat, Saltie Girl is its glamorous, city-slicker cousin. This stylish Back Bay restaurant slings some of the best seafood on Newbury Street, in an elegant yet playful dining room overlooking the boutiques of Newbury Street. Its classic New England-style lobster rolls arrive perfectly coiffed, alongside a charmingly branded bag of Saltie Girl potato chips (add some caviar from the raw bar if you like). But the real insider move here? Ask your server about the secret, off-menu version of the lobster roll: the meat comes fried, sprinkled with Korean chili flakes and sweet corn butter, resulting in something richer, spicier, and considerably more decadent than a traditional version. It’s a sterling reminder that, even in a historic city like Boston, we don’t have to take our classics so seriously. The Banks Seafood and Steak The Banks is a crowd-pleaser of a restaurant—a perfect location in Back Bay, a lively bar scene, and an elevated menu of New England classics. The lobster roll here is an example of a perfectly adventurous recipe where the chef has improved on the original with a few tweaks, but none so heretical that they feel like a major departure from tradition. It comes on a house-made brown-butter bun, sprinkled with sea salt and chives, and served with Old Bay potato chips. The hot lobster roll is a standout—it’s par-cooked, then warmed in a “lobster beurre monté,” a classic French technique that glazes the meat and also helps infuse more lobster flavor into it. The result is a roll that is deceptively simple, yes, bursting with flavor. Eventide Fenway Originally from Portland, Maine, Eventide brought its contemporary take on New England seafood to the Fenway neighborhood as a seafood counter in 2017 before evolving into a full-service restaurant in 2023. The experience here is decidedly more Boston than Maine—it’s a bustling, popular spot for pre-Fenway Park drinks and snacks, less of a cozy, James Beard-recognized eatery than its progenitor in Portland—but Eventide did one key invention with it for the Hub: its brown butter lobster rolls. They come on a fluffy, bao-style steamed bun, drenched (in a good way) with browned butter and flecked with sliced chives. The Sail Loft Nestled on the fringes of the North End within steps of the Freedom Trail, Faneuil Hall and the restaurants of Hanover Street, this institution feels like it’s been here forever. The Boston Sail Loft’s lobster roll is classic, with chilled lobster salad lightly dressed with mayonnaise and piled generously into a toasted bun. The thick, crispy fries that accompany it are a departure from the canonical bag of chips, but they’re a nice touch. There are fancier lobster rolls in Boston—but with perfect execution, stiff drinks and waterfront views, what else would you need? Red’s Best at Boston Public Market A great, no-frills option for travelers who want to understand where their seafood actually comes from, this counter inside Boston Public Market is dedicated to small, independent New England fishermen. And that direct connection to the local fishing community is what makes this experience special. The market itself—just steps from the Freedom Trail—is an easy stop while sightseeing, especially if you’re in the Faneuil Hall, North End, or Beacon Hill areas. The lobster rolls fresh and unfussy. While there’s no waterfront view or white tablecloth, there is something very Boston about enjoying solid seafood in a bustling public market surrounded by Bostonians going about their everyday lives. Plus: Save room for a doughnut from Union Square Donuts, or a popover from The Popover Lady. The Barking Crab Right across Fort Point Channel from James Hook & Co., you’ll find The Barking Crab, another old-school spot where the lobster rolls are classic, but the atmosphere is decidedly more festive. This ramshackle seafood restaurant feels like a relic from the old Seaport, before the neighborhood redeveloped into an epicenter of glass towers and luxury condos. The location makes it especially appealing on warmer days, and the vibe is a little rowdy (in a good way). The lobster roll here is a straightforward expression—toasted roll, available either tossed with mayo or “naked” with warm, butter-poached lobster meat—but if you’re really feeling like splurging, opt for the “One and Done”: whereas most rolls come with about one-fourth a pound of meat, this one comes with a solid one pound, for a whopping $150. Worth it? After a few beers or cocktails, you bet. Yankee Lobster Co. Venture into the Seaport, keep cruising past all the newfangled developments, and you’ll eventually find yourself at Yankee Lobster Co., which has been serving seafood here for roughly 75 years, making it one of the increasingly rare links to the city’s working waterfront in this part of town. That history is part of the appeal, and the lobster roll is comfortingly old-school: generously portioned, straightforward, crafted from the freshest lobster. Come here if you want a classic Boston seafood experience without the polish or price tags of the Seaport’s flashier restaurants. Sullivan’s Castle Island A visit to Castle Island—which is actually not an island, but the tip of the peninsula known as South Boston, or “Southie”—is a beloved Boston ritual. You walk or bike to the far edge of Southie, go for a waterfront stroll around Fort Independence, the oldest continuously fortified site in British North America, then stop for a refueling at Sullivan’s, so much a part of the fabric of Boston life that it received a James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award. This is not the lobster roll to choose if you’re looking for culinary drama—it’s the one you choose when you want to eat seafood like a Boston local.

item.title: You Can Now Book the 'Sterling Point' Cottage on Airbnb—and the Inside Might Surprise You
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.41
Great news for anyone who fell in love with Muskoka after watching Sterling Point but didn't inherit a lake house from their estranged grandfather: Gordon Bay Cottage, the actual property at the center of the hit show, is officially coming to Airbnb. In the Prime Video series, protagonist Annie Rubin makes a pilgrimage to the property—located on a fictional island called Sterling Point—after finding out it has been willed to her after the death of her grandfather, Gordon. Now, fans will be able to call this same cottage home, at least for a few nights, thanks to an Airbnb sweepstakes allowing guests to request one of three special stays at the five-bedroom lakeside lodge this fall. Bookings open on September 15 at 9 a.m. ET, and the stays will take place October 2 to 5, October 9 to 12, and October 16 to 19, with a price tag of $180 a night. If you're looking to cosplay as Annie, Ellis, Connor, or Ramona, set your alarm now—these dates are going to go quick. While Gordon Bay Cottage serves as the façade for Gordon's cottage, interior scenes were filmed on a soundstage in Toronto, about two hours south of Muskoka. That means while the outside of the home will look familiar—cedar-shingled gables, wraparound porch, stone steps leading down to the water, Muskoka chair–dotted dock—the interiors aren't what you'd expect. In fact, they're way more upscale. While Gordon's place in the show looks like it hasn't been updated in a few decades, the property up for grabs on Airbnb appears fresh and modern, with hardwood floors, bright white walls, and contemporary but comfortable furniture. Probably not Ramona's style, but definitely ideal for a luxurious long weekend on the lake. The real Gordon Bay Cottage also sits right on Lake Joseph, one of the most popular and sought-after lakes in the Muskoka region, which means a stay here will come with all the trappings of a classic Canadian summer getaway. Sweepstakes winners should come with their Roots sweatpants and be prepared to “shower” in the lake, drink some Steam Whistles around the firepit, drive their boats to dinner, and gulp down some fresh air while staring at the stars. Ready to experience all that cottage country has to offer but afraid you won't be able to score a stay at Gordon Bay Cottage? Lucky for you, there are plenty of other incredible rentals in Muskoka, and we've found the best of the best. Between Sterling Point, Heated Rivalry, and Every Year After, this stunning slice of Ontario is more popular than ever (no, really, Airbnb searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 are up nearly 110% year over year, according to the vacation rental brand), so if you want to secure a lakeside spot for next summer, you'd be wise to start looking—and booking—now.
