item.title: 11 National Parks That Are Even More Beautiful in the Fall
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.26
I’ve traveled far and wide through America’s national parks, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some landscapes are simply better with a little fall color. Come September and October, sweeping valleys turn gold, forests flare in riots of red and pops of orange, and high country trails welcome that crisp, exhilarating drop in temperature that makes you want to keep trekking a little farther. Even parks we know and love in summer feel completely transformed: the sunsets shine differently, wildlife activity changes, and the seasonal crowds begin to give way to a quieter, more immersive experience. Thanks to the breadth of terrain across the US national parks, there’s no single version of how to experience fall. You might be leaf-peeping beneath the peaks of the Tetons, winding through Acadia’s brilliant coastal forests, hiking Yosemite in the cooler weather, or watching the aspens flicker across the Rockies. And when the sun goes down, the day doesn’t have to end: there are campfires to linger around, stars to seek out, and hot springs to slip into. Below, I’ve rounded up 11 national parks that are particularly spectacular in autumn. Take note: Fall may be shoulder season, but don’t assume that means easy availability—lodges, campgrounds, permits, and popular activities can still book up, so check current park conditions and reservation requirements before you go. —Jessica Chapel This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 16 Best Resorts on Private Islands for an Ultra-Exclusive Getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.23
For many, true relaxation looks like dropping off the map—settling down on a secluded, sparsely populated island where no one knows anything about you, save for your favorite tropical cocktail. The very best private island resorts balance downtime and adventure; personal space and hospitality; rugged, natural beauty and state-of-the-art facilities. Scattered across the turquoise waters of Indonesia, the Maldives, and Turks and Caicos, some of these properties are wonderfully far-flung, while others, like Little Palm Island Resort & Spa in Florida and Lovango Resort and Beach Club in the US Virgin Islands, don’t even require a US passport. No matter where you decide to book your bungalow, you can rest assured that exclusivity and quietude take top priority at the properties on this list. Offering everything from fresh meals tailored to your preferences to bespoke spa treatments, these resorts are built on the idea that it’s all for you. Whether you’re seeking an open-air villa that floats above crystal-clear water, a luxury ecolodge powered by wind turbines, or a safari-style escape where jungle hikes are always on the table, these are the world’s best private island resorts—each the very definition of paradise. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tetiaroa, French Polynesia Actor Marlon Brando’s legacy lives on at his former private getaway in French Polynesia, now a hyper-exclusive, eco-minded retreat where travelers come to escape it all. Relax in one of 35 stylish, palm-thatched villas, each a grand fusion of indoor and outdoor space, the beach just footsteps away (alternatively, go even bigger with the island’s sole over-the-top residence). Enjoy island bike rides, treatments in the stickwork cocoons of the Varua te Ora Polynesian Spa, and French-tinged, Polynesian-influenced dining by French celebrity chef Jean Imbert. Nature tours led by in-house researchers offer a deeper connection to the island, while daily cultural experiences like Polynesian dance classes, ukulele lessons, and traditional weaving sessions introduce guests to local traditions. Make sure to save time to explore the other islands of the Tetiaroa Atoll, which also belong to the Brando family, where untouched beaches, preserved reefs, and thriving seabird colonies are as gorgeous as when Brando first encountered the location in 1960. All meals, libations (including Champagne), in-room dining, and daily spa treatments are bundled into the all-inclusive rate, allowing for carefree indulgence at every turn. And although The Brando immerses guests in barefoot ultra-luxury, it also quietly stands as one of the world’s most sustainable resorts—powered by solar energy and cooled by innovative seawater systems—preserving the paradise Brando so deeply loved for generations to come. —Antonia Quirke - Read Full ReviewLocation: Little Torch Key, Florida This adults-only private island is a study in tropical chic, redefining the castaway fantasy right on American soil. There are a total of 30 thatched-roof bungalow suites (some freestanding, some within larger bungalows) across the four-acre island, many with four-poster beds and outdoor copper bathtubs. Thanks to a smart layout and smarter landscaping, you’ll encounter other people less often than you’d expect (a strict cap at 60 guests helps). All suites have water views, outdoor showers, and furnished decks; most also overlook private slivers of white-sand beach and are kitted out with hammocks, loungers, and firepits. The Dining Room has sweeping sea views, and the spectacular SpaTerre complex is underscored by a breezy two-story atrium. Paddleboard or kayak through mangrove mazes as eagle rays swim by, laze the day away on a beachfront hammock, or simply enjoy the day resting on a poolside lounger. Also, don’t miss a snorkeling trip to Looe Key Reef, part of the third-largest living coral reef in the world and site of ongoing reef restoration efforts by MOTE Marine Laboratory & Aquarium, a Florida-based nonprofit marine research institution. Little Palm Island has partnered with the organization to create the “Paradise with a Purpose” package, which includes a half-day in Looe Key Reef, a donation to MOTE Marine, accommodations, and breakfast. —Paul Rubio - Read Full ReviewLocation: Yaukuve Levu Island, Fiji Located in the untouched Kadavu Islands, a 45-minute seaplane flight from Nadi International Airport, this private island balances romance and multigenerational travel in Fiji. Straddling the renowned Great Astrolabe Reef, the waters near Kokomo teem with colorful fish, manta rays, sea turtles, and thriving coral gardens, making underwater exploration a must for any visit (don’t miss the marine biologist–led manta snorkel excursion). Twenty-one beachfront villas range in size from a couples-friendly one-bedroom to larger two- and three-bedrooms, each with a private plunge pool, private walled garden with outdoor shower, and direct beach access. Meanwhile, five hilltop luxury Grand Residences welcome larger families to multi-bedroom homes, inclusive of a private butler and nanny. Guests can also anticipate other water activities like sailing and kayaking, and three memorable meals daily, made of locally sourced produce from Kokomo’s 5.5-acre farm and hydroponics garden, and seafood from a sustainable, caught-to-order island initiative. —Adam H. Graham - Read Full ReviewLocation: Anambas, Indonesia There are drop-dead gorgeous private island resorts, and then there’s Bawah, an entire nature and marine reserve comprising 6 islands, 3 blue lagoons, and 13 unspoiled white beaches in the heart of Indonesia’s Anambas Archipelago. Sustainability lies at the core of the reserve with no compromises on luxury. In fact, the entire resort was constructed by hand using sustainable bamboo and locally sourced natural building materials, and decorated with works from local artisans. The reserve oozes natural splendor, which can be enjoyed from the comfort of a swoon-worthy rustic-chic tented suite, overwater bungalow, or pool villa. Come here for Indonesian coastal cuisine perfected, dinners in the treetops, spectacular sunsets, hikes through the jungle, island-hopping via transparent kayaks, and sublime snorkeling. To access Bawah’s remote location with ease, the reserve offers a door-to-door transfer from Singapore airport with short components by road and ferry, followed by a 75-minute seaplane that lands directly in paradise. —Michelle Jana Chan - Read Full ReviewLocation: Peter Island, British Virgin Islands From the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island, the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, turns up the volume on the wellness-minded, pastoral strains of Caribbean life, and in no time, you might just find yourself humming along to the tune. With just 52 rooms and 2 villas, you’ll never have to battle for privacy and discretion, yet the company of fellow guests is always welcome. In 2017, Hurricane Irma tragically destroyed homes and upended lives throughout the Virgin Islands. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75% of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavor of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favorite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. —Kat Chen - Read Full ReviewLocation: Mnemba Island, Tanzania Just shy of two miles off the coast of Zanzibar’s main island, Mnemba is a tiny, casuarina-forested sanctuary surrounded by a private marine reserve. Home to just 12 shell-shaped, thatched bandas, designed with understated elegance by Fox Browne Creative and Jack Alexander Studio, it’s the antithesis of bling. A seven-month rebuild in 2024 expanded the villas into curvaceous, nautilus-like spaces, blending natural materials with breezy open-air design. Guests can explore turquoise shallows on catamarans, dive vibrant reefs, or simply lounge in private beach bandas watching noddies and plovers whirl above the sandspit. The spa, yoga deck, and Oceans Without Borders education center enrich the experience, while chefs curate custom menus that range from sushi boxes to lobster ravioli served under the stars. Service is impeccable, with a charming butler, a jovial bar team, and Tanzania’s first local dive master leading ocean explorations. Despite Zanzibar’s tourism boom, Mnemba feels like a world apart—exclusive, untouched, and deeply serene. With a staff-to-guest ratio of over 3:1, every detail is handled, leaving you to do exactly what you’re meant to here: absolutely nothing. —Lisa Grainger - Read Full ReviewLocation: Nosy Ankao, Madagascar A nothing-is-impossible hideaway for adventurous high-fliers, Miavana by Time + Tide is set on remote Nosy Ankao in northern Madagascar, only reachable by helicopter. With ease, the private island merges barefoot luxury and a deep commitment to conservation and community support. Just 14 villas, built from sun-bleached Malagasy wood and hand-hewn limestone, sprawl across private gardens and powder-soft beaches. Interiors channel a beachy Palm Springs vibe, with sunken bathtubs, pastel Smeg appliances, and fully stocked kitchens, offering a luxurious home-away-from-home feeling. The central Piazza serves farm-fresh menus that change daily, while off-menu requests are happily fulfilled. Though there’s no stand-alone spa, therapists deliver seashell massages and herbal body wraps directly to your villa. Service is breezy yet impeccable, with butlers anticipating every need—whether folding laundry, crafting green juices, or lending sunglasses. Miavana by Time + Tide’s eco-efforts are serious: villas rely on natural ventilation, solar panels power much of the resort, and local conservation programs protect turtles, lemurs, and coral reefs. While private island life is great, take time to explore mainland Madagascar’s iconic baobab forests or Tsingy formations (both can be arranged by helicopter safari from the island). —Chris Schalkx - Read Full ReviewLocation: Islas Secas, Panama Set within the jungle-cloaked splendor of Panama’s Gulf of Chiriquí, Islas Secas offers an exclusive, eco-friendly escape across a private archipelago of 14 untouched islands. At its heart, the resort’s eight light-footed accommodations—including casitas, safari-style tents, and open-air mansion Casa Cavada—blend flawlessly into the landscape, each with sweeping hilltop views and living spaces that celebrate the outdoors. Guests have exclusive access to this entire island chain, blanketed in tropical flora and fringed by white- and gold-sand beaches. Days unfold as you please across the various islands: kayak through emerald waters, snorkel vibrant coral gardens, hike jungle trails to ancient artifacts, or island-hop to wide, sparkling beaches where staff can arrange private beach barbecues. Water adventures abound, too, from fun on pricey water toys like hydrofoils, flyboards, and Seabobs, to fishing and whale-watching, all included in the resort’s personalized, all-inclusive program. On the main island of Isla Cavada, find a stunning open-air beachfront restaurant, a swoon-worthy jungle spa, a Hemingway-inspired bar, and an infinity pool perched high above the rainforest coastline. —Andrea Whittle - Read Full ReviewLocation: Necker Island, British Virgin Islands Necker Island is the creation of Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson, who has transformed what was once a scrubby, 74-acre British Virgin Island cay into a fortress of lush greenery, serene Balinese villas, exotic animals ranging from local flamingos to endangered lemurs and tortoises, and solar panels and wind turbines that make the island self-sustaining. The resort is accessible only by boat from nearby Tortola—no private-plane runway here—which makes it feel more approachable and refuge-like, especially compared to some other private-island hospitality projects. Every inch of the place feels like a Bond hideaway: Tropical canopies give way to white-sand beaches all your own, lagoons filled with flamingos, infinity-pooled suites, and cozy lounges. A sprawling hilltop Great House has far-flung views of the azure waters around the island; there's also a billiards table, board games, a bar (just one of many on the island, including the self-serve one in your own villa), and dining nooks with incredible views where five-star, family-style dinners and healthy à la carte breakfasts are served. —Shannon McMahon - Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos Located off the main chain of Turks and Caicos, Ambergris Cay achieves billionaire-level relaxation with its serene azure waters, rugged nature, and waterfront villas. The 1,100-acre island is home to a collection of expansive villas, from 1-bedroom beachfront bungalows to 10-bedroom homes. All meals and house beverages are included, meaning you’ll never go hungry—or thirsty—with cocktails made from fresh ingredients and a floating rum bar called The Hangover accessible only by boat. Suites sit on the sugar-sand beach leading into the Caribbean Sea, while sprawling villas are perched on craggy hilltops overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Interiors are beach house chic, with wood-plank floors and shiplap walls. Guests roam the island via golf cart between the spa, tennis courts, beach activities, and state-of-the-art fitness center encased in 180 degrees of glass. Service is breezy but attentive, with 24/7 concierge support via WhatsApp. The private island resort also houses one of the longest runways in the region, making it easy for outdoor-minded billionaires and professional athletes to arrive in private jets for instant immersion into the tropical good life. —S.M. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lovango Cay, US Virgin Islands Located across St. John’s legendary Caneel Bay on an island all its own, this unpretentious seasonal resort (open December through July) features the USVI’s only private island beach club and eco-chic accommodation in the form of wooden treehouses, explorer-style tents, and one- to three-bedroom villas. Views of the surrounding jewel-toned waters abound, peaking at Treetops Lobby Tent, where bird's-eye views of St. John proper and St. Thomas can be admired in a single panorama. Indulge in island cuisine and rum-spiked fun at the resort’s Waterfront Restaurant (get the smoked pineapple old- fashioned and the signature Caribbean lobster paillard) or its fast-casual counterpart, Sand Pit, which services Lovango’s Beach Club and its cabana-lined swimming pool. For active and gastronomic pursuits in greater St. John, take the ferry to Cruz Bay, which runs regularly; for another incarnation of beach bliss, hop on the five-minute ferry to St. John’s Honeymoon Beach, which runs on select days. —Todd Plummer - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lhaviyani Atoll, Maldives This Yuji Yamazaki–designed property in the Maldives’s Lhaviyani Atoll is a next-generation ultra-luxury experience like no other, underscored by a mind-blowing “Anything, Anytime, Anywhere” fixed price policy, where few things are off-limits—nor cost extra—from floating breakfasts to most top-shelf Champagne to private fitness training. The island’s 15 ryokan-inspired overwater residences epitomize contemporary Japanese ocean elegance, offering ample room to relax and play against the backdrop of the Maldives’ lazuline beauty (units start at 3,300 square feet). At Kudadoo’s core lies The Retreat, an impressive open-air minimalist overwater pagoda crowned by 984 solar panels (that power the resort in its entirety) and housing the island’s bar, restaurant, spa, fitness facilities, and lounge areas. Thanks to the Anything, Anytime, Anywhere policy, your residence, The Retreat, and the surrounding nature become your muses for fulfilling the utmost island fantasies. Request to be marooned on nearby Dream Island for a luxury-draped Robinson Crusoe experience or ask for a private toes-in-the-sand beach lunch on Kudadoo itself. Snorkel with giant mantas alongside a marine biologist or try your hand at jet-skiing, parasailing, or fishing. Pencil in plenty of time for spa treatments—they are unlimited, after all—before or after you figure out how to manage an entire staff of butlers, cooks, personal trainers, and yoga masters at your beck and call. Suffice to say, Kudadoo is the ultimate castaway narrative come to life—and the script is yours to write. —L.G. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Moskito Island, British Virgin Islands While everyone knows about billionaire Richard Branson’s original private retreat, Necker Island, the Virgin founder purchased another exclusive playground just two miles away called Moskito Island. But instead of using it for himself and his high-powered pals, the mogul built a home and sold nine other plots for others to build their dream beach houses. While most are only inhabited by the estate owners themselves, three of the remarkable properties—The Branson Estate, The Oasis Estate, and The Point Estate—became available for rent in October 2021. Although more expensive than your average luxury hotel, Moskito Island makes living the life of a billionaire a tiny bit more accessible. Five-star restaurants are swapped for private chefs, hotel suites for exclusive estates, and concierges for dedicated house managers capable of making nearly anything you want possible. The only guests in sight are those in your immediate party—that is, unless you decide to venture to the communal Manchioneel Beach, complete with a floating trampoline and bartenders at the ready, or the Beach House, a community recreational area where you can play a round of tennis and mingle with estate owners (you may even spot Richard Branson himself). —Jordi Lippe-McGraw - Gold List 2018, 2019, 2020Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos As COMO’s sole property in the Americas, Parrot Cay's renowned luxury experience makes it an unrivaled property in Turks and Caicos. The pinnacle of bespoke solitude, it's located on a private island enmeshed in the wilderness. You arrive after a 15-minute chauffeured drive from Providenciales International Airport, then a 20-minute panoramic boat ride through cays and turquoise waves hugged by mangroves. It’s primeval in nature and worlds away, despite its ease of access from the main island. The private, white-sand beach—with miles of clear-water sandbars inviting you to walk across, float around, and laze about for ages—is the main reason why the property has been dubbed by locals as "the Maldives of the Americas," despite being entirely singular in the impression it makes. If you’re seeking a romantic getaway inspired by an itch for an immersive nature escape, this is the place to go—and I recommend booking a private beach house with your own plunge pool for the full immersive experience. —Bridget Knowles FAQ: How we choose the best private island resorts in the world Every resort on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. item.title: The ultimate guide to finding 20°C+ sunshine all year – without a long-haul flight
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.17
As summer in the UK simmers to an end, our collective eyes start to wander, considering where we can find a much-needed boost of Vitamin D once dark evenings and wet mornings roll around. There are, of course, the winter sun big-hitters: Thailand for Christmas; the Maldives at New Year's; the Caribbean for a hit of February sunshine. But if you're clever, you can find little pockets of sunshiny joy closer to home all year-long. For true sun-seekers, this is your calendar of how to chase the sun from January to December – without ever boarding a flight for more than four hours. January: Lanzarote, Spain Average January temperature: daytime highs of 22°C The wild coastline of Lanzarote might not register on the radars of those left with the (wrong!) impression that this Canary Island is still a place for soulless package holidays. All the better for those who know better – that hangover from the ‘70s means that when this dramatic volcanic island reveals its true beauty, it comes as something of a joyful surprise. There’s a thriving artsy scene, a smart clutch of cool boutique hotels (we particularly like Cesar Lanzarote) to check into, and unspoilt beaches to explore. In January, expect minimal rainfall and daytime highs in the low 20s (although pack for cooler, breezy nights). February: Madeira, Portugal Average February temperature: daytime highs of 20°C The archipelago of Madeira, cast away off the coast of Portugal, is known for its subtropical climate (meaning hot summers and, crucially, mild winters), as well as its eponymous wine and craggy landscapes. There are also some fabulous hotels to check into – Reid's Palace, A Belmond Hotel, has a knockout pool carved into the coastline and acres of colourful gardens; while Savoy Palace is the smart choice for those looking for an all-inclusive fly-and-flop. February isn't peak season to visit, which means fewer crowds, but temperatures can still skim into the low 20s in the day, and any rainfall is short and sharp. March: Seville, Spain Average March temperature: daytime highs of 21°C The Andalucian city of Seville is a favourite among many Traveller editors – for its old-school restaurant scene, where the best mealtimes are spent hopping between bars, eating melty slithers of Jamón Ibérico washed down with white wine while stood at the bar of a tiled taberna; for the gorgeous Moorish architecture; and for the weather, which promises positivity for much of the year. I've visited twice, once in late October, and once in February: both were warm enough to sip sherry on the street and wander the orange-scented gardens at a leisurely pace, so I feel confident vouching for March, when the afternoons will be balmy without the intense heat that blankets the city in summer. April: Crete, Greece Average April temperature: daytime highs of 21°C The biggest Greek island is, some say, at its best in spring. Emerging from a surprisingly chilly winter, by April you can expect daytime temperatures around 21°C (by the end of the month, perhaps skimming the mid-20s) as well as blossoming flora and fauna. Local hotelier Nikos Tsepetis recently shared his guide to Crete's green heart during spring, without the crowds with us – after skimming for inspiration, check the best hotels in Crete for somewhere smart to stay. May: Malta Average May temperature: daytime highs of 24°C By May, much of Europe has defrosted, promising sunny days and warmer temperatures. Take your pick of destinations – ours is the island of Malta, beloved for its honey-hued Baroque capital city, Valletta, its glittering swimming spots and its enviable climate – Malta gets more than 300 days of sunshine every year. Wandering around the cobbled, UNESCO-listed streets, it's obvious why so many Hollywood productions have chosen the islands as their backdrop: spot them doubling as Ancient Rome in Gladiator and King's Landing in Game of Thrones. June: Alentejo, Portugal Average June temperature: daytime highs of 27°C Portugal's Alentejo region is a place to make the most of summer by slowing down and living a little better. Here, you won't find the crowds you might expect in other corners of the country in peak season: instead, you'll find peaceful countryside, golden-tinged rolling farms, pretty little villages like UNESCO-listed Évora, and a thriving food scene that spotlights traditional dishes, farm-to-table cooking (and not in a performative, zeitgeisty way) and local produce (and wine!). In June, days are warm without hitting the mega-temperatures starting to appear in other parts of Europe. July: Sweden Average July temperature: daytime highs of 22°C If there's one fantasy the Traveller editors keep rehashing at the moment, it's the idea of a Scandi summer – somewhere it's sunny but not too hot; where the days are long and spent soaking up nature without the crowds. Enter the archipelago of Sweden. Summer here is a jumble of bike rides, swimming in lakes, boat trips and festivals. August: Tallinn, Estonia Average August temperature: daytime highs of 22°C As one of the oldest cities in Europe, Tallinn is – perhaps unsurprisingly – drastically pretty. The Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There's a thriving food scene here – the best restaurants in Tallinn reflect the best of Estonia's produce and traditional recipes. In the summer, head up Toompea Hill for widescreen views of the city, take part in Tallinn's sauna culture or take a waterfront cycle. September: Athens, Greece Average September temperature: daytime highs of 29°C After a long, steamy summer, the Greek capital starts to emerge into the (relatively) cooler autumnal months in September. That still means temperatures close to 30°C at the beginning of the month, nine and a half hours of sunshine a day, and positively balmy sea temperatures of 25°C. Spend a long weekend in Athens seeing the Acropolis, wandering around Plaka, the oldest neighbourhood in the city, or culture-hopping around the brilliant museums. The best hotels in Athens, for our money, include The Dolli in the city and Four Seasons Astir Palace Hotel Athens on the Athenian Riviera. October: Sicily, Italy Average October temperature: daytime highs of 24°C The Italian island of Sicily is at its best in the autumn. The sea is at its most inviting, having been warmed by the blazing Mediterranean sun all summer long. Many of the crowds are gone, but there's still a buzz about the coastal towns like Taormina, made (more) famous by The White Lotus, and frenetic cities like Palermo. Our pick of the top hotels in Sicily: Villa Sant'Andrea, A Belmond Hotel, for an enviable seafront setting and Braccialieri Val di Noto for a bright, cheery stay. November: Southern Turkey Average November temperature: daytime highs of 21°C Turkey’s glitzy southern coast draws sunseekers all year long. Peak season might be over by the time November rolls around (bringing with it puffer-jacket and brolly weather at home), but the weather in some of our favourite spots like Bodrum is still enviable enough to tempt us for one final jaunt on these shores. Check into a perennial Traveller favourite, Macakizi, and forget about the winter blues for a few days. December: Malaga, Spain Average December temperature: daytime highs of 19°C Finding genuinely hot weather in Europe by the time we're nearing Christmas isn't easy. But there are corners to seek out where the climate is far better than our own. Case in point: the southern Spanish city of Malaga, where mild winter sun is all but guaranteed and rain is sparse. The city goes all-out for Christmas, with impressive festive lights and sweet Christmas markets to explore without the crowds.

item.title: What Backpacker Splurges in Thailand Really Cost
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.18
Backpacking through Thailand has earned a legendary reputation for being incredibly cheap. You can easily find five-dollar hostel beds, tasty two-dollar plates of Pad Thai on street corners, and overnight buses that take you across the country for next to nothing. However, after following a strict daily budget for a few weeks, almost every tourist reaches a point where they want to trade instant noodles and shared dorms for a special experience. Thailand is one of the best places in the world to treat yourself because your money goes much further here than back home. If you wonder what major budget splurges cost now, here is a realistic look at popular activities, from scaling limestone cliffs in Krabi to teeing off at Thailand's top golf courses. Popular Activities in Thailand Rock Climbing on the Cliffs of Railay Beach Railay Beach in Krabi Province is world-famous among outdoor enthusiasts. Towering limestone karsts rise straight out of turquoise waters, creating some of the most dramatic climbing routes on the planet. Even without climbing experience, local gear shops make it safe and easy to get onto the rock face. A half-day guided climbing program in Railay costs 1,200 to 1,800 Thai Baht ($36 to $55 USD). This covers all equipment, including harness fitting, special shoes, chalk, a guide, and climbing on beginner-friendly walls such as Muay Thai Wall or Diamond Cave. If you want to climb multi-pitch routes on the Thaiwand Wall, it will cost approximately 6,500 to 9,000 Baht ($198 to $274). Budget an extra 100 to 150 Baht ($3 to $4.50) each way for the longtail boat ride from Ao Nang Pier because Railay is cut off from roads by giant cliffs. Getting PADI Scuba Certified in Koh Tao or Phuket If you want to dive beneath the waves, taking a scuba course in Thailand is a rite of passage for travelers. The small island of Koh Tao is one of Thailand's most affordable places to get your PADI Open Water certification. The full price for the Open Water Course lasting more than one day at Koh Tao is 9,500 to 11,000 Baht ($280 to $325). It includes classroom theory, pool dives, four ocean dives, and gear rental. If you take the certification course in Phuket or Koh Lanta, the cost is slightly higher, ranging from 12,000 to 14,000 Baht ($350 to $410) due to larger dive boats and marine park entry fees. For certified divers who want a single day of fun diving, a two-tank boat trip typically costs 3,200 to 4,200 Baht ($94 to $123) and usually includes a freshly cooked hot lunch on the boat deck. Teeing Off on Championship Golf Courses Near Bangkok When people think of backpacker trips, golf usually does not come to mind. Yet Thailand is a top destination for golf lovers thanks to its immaculate fairways and attentive service. Taking a break from urban exploring to play 18 holes near Bangkok is one of the most fun and unique day trips to add to an itinerary. At Green Valley Country Club near Suvarnabhumi Airport on the Bangna-Trad highway, current green fees are approximately 1,200 Baht ($36) on weekdays, 2,500 Baht ($75) for twilight play, and 4,000 Baht ($122) on weekends. The course is designed by Robert Trent Jones Jr., with massive water features and premium-quality greens that deliver a high-end experience without private-club price tags. Golfers should budget about 850 Baht ($26) for a cart, 450 Baht ($14) for the compulsory caddie, and a customary tip of 400 Baht ($12). That puts the approximate cost of an 18-hole round at 2,900 to 5,700 Baht ($88 to $173) before transportation or club rental. Rates vary by date, tee time, and booking method. Confirm the total before booking. Visiting an Ethical Elephant Sanctuary in Chiang Mai Visiting Chiang Mai provides an opportunity to experience Asian elephants firsthand. It is vital to select an ethical sanctuary that does not involve riding but focuses on rescue, rehabilitation, and natural eating habits. Sanctuaries such as Elephant Nature Park are the benchmark for animal conservation. The average cost of a tour at a reputable sanctuary is 2,500 to 3,500 Baht ($76 to $106). The price covers transportation in a van between the sanctuary and your Chiang Mai hotel, a vegetarian lunch, and time with the rescued elephants, including walking with them, preparing their food, and watching them bathe in local rivers. Although the tour costs more than a temple tour, it is worth every Baht because it helps animals in need. Living Large for a Day Is Worth Every Penny Backpacking does not mean skipping incredible life experiences to save a few dollars. By balancing budget street food and dorm rooms with one or two well-chosen bucket-list adventures, you get the best of both worlds in Thailand. Whether you climb giant cliffs, explore underwater reefs, or spend a quiet morning on a sunny fairway, these mid-trip splurges often become highlights you talk about for years after returning home. item.title: Kilimanjaro Routes Compared: Which Should You Choose?
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.69
Seven official routes lead up Kilimanjaro, and most people narrow their choice to two or three within an hour of reading about them. Machame is the popular one, Lemosho the scenic one, Marangu the one where you sleep in huts instead of tents. Those labels are accurate but don't affect whether you reach the summit. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) high. Its standard trekking routes do not require technical climbing equipment (ropes, an ice axe), but the extreme altitude makes acclimatization essential. The number of days on the mountain matters. Five-day itineraries leave less time for acclimatization, while some operators report summit success rates around 95% on eight-day climbs. These are operator-reported figures, not mountain-wide averages. The takeaway is simple: allow your body more time to adapt before summit night. How the Routes Actually Work Seven official ascent routes exist, but they don't stay separate all the way up. Every climb has three phases, and the route you choose changes each of them differently. The approach (the first four to six days) is where the routes differ. Lemosho starts in quiet rainforest on the western flank. Rongai comes from the dry northern side near the Kenyan border. Machame and Marangu climb from the busy south. For four to six days, you circle toward Kibo, the main volcanic cone, gaining altitude through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert. This is where you acclimatize, so the number of days here matters most. Summit night. The approaches converge toward Kibo, with most standard itineraries using one of two main summit routes. If you came via Machame, Lemosho, Shira, or Umbwe, you leave Barafu Camp around midnight, climb to Stella Point, then walk the crater rim to Uhuru Peak. Marangu and Rongai climbers leave Kibo Hut, and their route to Gilman's Point takes longer because much of it runs over loose volcanic scree. Either way, you gain about 1,200 meters in the dark. The Western Breach is another summit route, but rockfall and unstable ice make it risky. For that reason, careful operators avoid it. The descent. The park separates uphill and downhill traffic. Routes that summit from Barafu come down the Mweka corridor, a trail used only for going down. Marangu and Rongai climbers walk back down the Marangu trail, sharing it with groups heading up. The Routes, Side by Side | Route | Days | Start from | Sleeping | Traffic | Pick it if | | Machame ("Whiskey") | 7 (or 6) | South | Tents | High | You want the classic climb-high-sleep-low profile and the Barranco Wall, and crowds don't bother you. | | Lemosho | 8 (or 7) | West | Tents | Low early, medium later | It's your first high-altitude climb, and you can spare the extra day. | | Marangu ("Coca-Cola") | 6 (or 5) | Southeast | Wooden huts | High | Sleeping in a tent is not an option for you. | | Rongai | 6 | North | Tents | Low | You want quiet, or you're climbing during the short rains. | | Northern Circuit | 8–9 | West, then north | Tents | Very low | You prioritize extra acclimatization time and a quieter approach. | | Umbwe | 6 | South | Tents | Very low | You're already acclimatized and want a steep, direct route. | | Londorossi (Shira) | 6–8 | West, by vehicle to the plateau | Tents | Very low | You want open views from day one and understand the altitude trade-off. | Route by Route Machame: the "Whiskey Route" (7 days) Machame is the most popular route on the mountain, and the nickname compares it to Marangu, the "Coca-Cola Route." The key differences are that Machame is tougher and steeper, and you sleep in tents. In seven days, you pass through every climate zone Kilimanjaro has, from wet rainforest at 1,800 meters to the frozen crater rim. The third day takes you up to Lava Tower at 4,600 meters and then down to Barranco Camp at 3,900 meters to sleep. That is the "climb high, sleep low" principle built into the route, which is why Machame acclimatizes people so well despite its pace. The next morning you scramble the Barranco Wall, a near-vertical face that needs hands for balance but no rope. The downside is traffic. Machame and Marangu take the lion's share of expeditions, and you will share camps with hundreds of other climbers. The Barranco Wall gives the climb real mountaineering character, and the scenery earns the route its reputation. Still, anyone choosing Machame has to be willing to move in a stream of other groups and share the intermediate camps. The other decision on Machame is between six and seven days. The difference is a single night at Karanga Camp after the Barranco Wall. Drop it, and you go straight from the wall to Barafu and into summit night on the same push, when accumulated fatigue shows up. For example, ALPO runs the Machame Route on the seven-day schedule and keeps that Karanga night for this reason; the company reports 95-97% of its climbers reaching the summit on that version. Its guidance on the six-day option is that the success rate is lower. Lemosho (8 days) Lemosho starts on the remote western flank at Londorossi Gate, about three hours' drive from Moshi. The first two days run through rainforest that the southern routes never touch, and you may not see another group. This is where you are most likely to see colobus monkeys. The route then crosses the Shira Plateau from west to east, one of the highest plateaus on Earth, and on the eight-day version you spend two nights up there, at Shira 1 (3,500 m) and Shira 2 (3,840 m). That slow gain is the whole point. From the plateau, Lemosho joins the Machame trail, so the Lava Tower day, the Barranco Wall, and the summit night are the same. The main decision on Lemosho is whether to do seven or eight days. Dropping to seven means crossing Shira in one long stage and losing a night of adaptation, which helps most. Lemosho also costs more than Machame, partly because of the long drive to a remote trailhead and partly because the extra day adds food and crew wages. For someone whose first real altitude climb is this one, the eight-day Lemosho remains the most balanced option; the gain comes slowly enough that your body has time to catch up. Marangu: the "Coca-Cola Route" (6 days) Marangu is the only route where you sleep in permanent wooden huts instead of tents. The huts are dorm-style, with anywhere from 4 to 20 people per room and shared bathrooms. It is also the historic original route and the one with the gentlest approach gradient, which is how it got its reputation as the easy one. That reputation can be misleading: a gentler trail does not remove altitude challenges. If you prefer hut accommodation, compare daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities carefully, and favor the six-day itinerary over the five-day version. Summit night climbs from Kibo Hut toward Gilman's Point, and the route uses the same trail for ascent and descent, so you meet descending groups on your way up. The sensible rule is to choose Marangu in exactly one case, when a tent is physically or psychologically not an option for you, and then to take six days, never five. Rongai (6 days) Rongai approaches from the north, close to the Kenyan border, after a long drive to the trailhead. The northern flank is drier, making Rongai the sensible pick if climbing during the short rains in November. It is also the quietest standard route, with a real chance of larger wildlife on the lower section. The early terrain is less dramatic than on the western routes, and summit night from Kibo Hut is long and monotonous. It is probably the most undervalued route on the mountain: introverted, wild, and worth the trade for silence. Editor's note: For a firsthand perspective, read this account of climbing Kilimanjaro via the Rongai Route, from life at camp to the midnight summit push. Northern Circuit (8-9 days) The Northern Circuit is one of the longest itinerary options, giving you more time to acclimatize. As a result, it has one of the higher summit rates. It starts on the western side, like Lemosho, then swings around the northern face of Kibo on a nearly empty traverse before rejoining the main trails for the summit push. The extra days provide more time to adapt, although individual responses to altitude vary. It is generally among the more expensive options because you are paying for a longer expedition, and it requires solid multi-day trekking endurance. If reliably reaching Uhuru Peak is the goal and time is not the constraint, this is the route. Umbwe and Londorossi (Shira) Umbwe is the steepest line on the mountain and the most direct, climbing a narrow forest ridge that almost no one else uses. Its rapid ascent leaves little time to acclimatize, making it a better option for trekkers who are already acclimatized. Previous altitude experience alone is not a substitute. Londorossi, sometimes called the Shira Route, approaches from the west but begins with a vehicle transfer straight onto the Shira Plateau at 3,400 meters. The views open from day one. You give up the gradual gain that every other route builds in, which is worth considering before you book. What To Weigh Before You Book Days on the mountain. When comparing itineraries, prioritize acclimatization time. Look beyond total trip length to daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities. Extra time helps, but fitness and previous altitude experience do not guarantee protection from altitude illness. Follow your guide's safety advice and be prepared to turn around. That is not a guidebook opinion. Yevgen Staroselskiy, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions, is a Master of Sport in Mountaineering and holder of the "Snow Leopard" title (#376), with more than 130 major climbs behind him, including Everest (8,848 m, 29,029 ft) and K2 (8,611 m, 28,251 ft), and 25+ groups guided to the top of Kilimanjaro. His view of the time question is blunt: I've climbed Everest and K2, and I can tell you that no route on Kilimanjaro needs that kind of preparation. What it does need is that you take the altitude seriously. Give your body the days, walk slowly, and almost any physically active person will reach Uhuru Peak. Where I see people fail is when they try to save a day. - Yevgen Staroselskiy, Master of Sport in Mountaineering, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions Everything else on this list is secondary to that number. Tent or hut. A binary question, and it settles Marangu yes-or-no before anything else. Crowds. Machame and Marangu are busy. Rongai and the Northern Circuit are not. Lemosho is quiet for two days and then joins the Machame stream. Summit night profile. From Barafu, the climb to Stella Point is steeper, but you are mostly on firm ground. From Kibo Hut, you spend more hours on scree before you reach Gilman's Point. Season. Compare expected rainfall and trail conditions for your travel dates with your operator. Wetter periods mean muddy trails and reduced visibility; the northern approach is generally drier. Conditions vary, so avoid treating any seasonal window as a guarantee of dry weather. The dry windows are June to early October and mid-December to early April. During the short rains in November, the northern side stays drier, which is a point in Rongai's favor. In April and May, the trails wash out, and clouds hide the views, so no route is worth doing then. A Quick Decision Guide - First high-altitude climb and you can spare eight days: Lemosho. - Seven days, and sharing camp with other groups does not bother you: Machame, on the seven-day schedule rather than six. - You will not sleep in a tent: Marangu, six days, no shorter. - Climbing in November, or you want the mountain mostly to yourself: Rongai. - More time for acclimatization and a quieter approach: Northern Circuit. Whichever route you choose, prioritize an itinerary that allows time to acclimatize rather than booking the shortest option. This article was published in partnership with ALPO Guided Expeditions.

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.29
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing. The contemplative alternatives are Naoshima and Teshima, neighboring art islands in the Seto Inland Sea: the Chichu Art Museum costs ¥2,500-3,000 with timed reservations that cap visitors. The Teshima Art Museum costs ¥1,800-2,000. The direct ferry from Uno Port to Naoshima costs ¥370, while the ferry to Teshima costs ¥780. Per ticket, the islands undercut teamLab. Per trip, they usually don't: Uno Port is a Shinkansen ride and two local connections from Tokyo, and that transport dwarfs the admission savings. The swap only makes financial sense when Setouchi is already on your route, say between Osaka and Hiroshima. If it is, take it without hesitation; if not, this is the case where the crowded option is genuinely the affordable one. The Cheapest Alternative: Don't Leave the City You're In The most expensive way to escape a crowd is to cross half of Honshu. A same-day dash from Tokyo to Kyoto for Fushimi Inari's torii gates costs over ¥28,000 in return shinkansen fares before you have eaten anything. Meanwhile, Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest, has its own tunnel of vermilion torii at the Otome Inari sub-shrine, costs nothing to enter, and sits a ¥180 metro ride from central Tokyo. The same logic covers bamboo. Kamakura's Hokoku-ji temple has a grove where you can sit with matcha for ¥400 admission plus ¥600 for the tea. The Great Buddha at Kotoku-in across town charges ¥300, and the train from Tokyo costs ¥1,040. That makes a full bamboo-and-Buddha day out possible for under ¥5,000, compared with visiting Arashiyama's grove at the far end of a ¥28,000 round trip. Even garden-hopping scales down: Kiyosumi Garden charges ¥150 for stone-hopping across carp ponds that Shinjuku Gyoen crowds pay ¥500 for. Altitude works the same way. Shibuya Sky's rooftop charges ¥2,700 online for daytime entry and ¥3,400 for sunset slots, and shares the deck with everyone else who booked the same golden hour. Sunshine 60's Tenbou-Park observatory in Ikebukuro shows a comparable skyline for ¥700 on weekdays, and the free 26th-floor observation lobby of Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, a few minutes from Shibuya on the Den-en-toshi line, faces Mount Fuji at sunset and charges nothing at all. Four Rules Before You Swap - Price the final leg first. Rural alternatives live or die by the last bus or ferry: its fare and, above all, its schedule. One missed daily departure can force a taxi that costs more than the whole day. - Admission is rarely the problem. Japanese entry fees are modest: ¥150-800 covers most of the attractions in this article. Accommodation and intercity trains decide your budget, so compare hotel rates and lodging taxes before temple tickets. For a broader breakdown of travel costs, read Go Backpacking's guide to backpacking Japan on a budget. - Some crowded icons are free. Fushimi Inari charges nothing; Shirakawa-go's lanes charge nothing. Swapping away from them buys you a better experience, not a cheaper one. Know which reward you're paying for. - Recheck prices from 2026 onward. The March 2026 JR East fare rise and Kyoto's doubled accommodation tax made many older budget guides inaccurate. The official links above reflect August 2026 prices. Quiet and cheap usually travel together in Japan, but not always, and never automatically. Run the numbers for your own route, and you'll often find the lesser-known option costs less and gives more. When it doesn't, at least you'll know before the bus timetable tells you.
