item.title: A Climber Was Stuck on a Stawamus Chief Cliff. A Flying Drone Delivered a Jacket and a Rope to Save Him.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.73
After 10 P.M. on September 10, Squamish Search and Rescue arrived at the Stawamus Chief, specifically on a climbing route known as the Alaska Highway (Photo: Courtesy of Squamish Search and Rescue) A highly specialized search-and-rescue drone team pulled off a bold late-night rescue in Squamish, British Columbia, Canada, after a climber found himself stranded on a cliff. The man was stuck standing on a ten-inch ledge 250 feet above the ground, secured to an anchor but without enough rope to descend. Squamish Search and Rescue sent in two aerial drones, one to light up the wall and provide a bird’s-eye view of the situation, and a second to deliver clothing, lights, and a climbing rope to the stricken climber. The rescue played out on Stawamus Chief, one of the world’s largest granite monoliths that is a hotbed for trad and face climbers. Dustin Wales, 36, is the drone program coordinator for the responding agency, Squamish Search and Rescue. He told Outside that his team spent the last two years preparing for a situation like this, training drone pilots and establishing protocols for any situation across rugged terrain, including this. “We just hadn’t had the opportunity to put this in action,” Wales said. After 10 P.M. on September 10, Squamish Search and Rescue arrived at the Stawamus Chief, where the stuck climber had been attempting a multi-pitch route called Alaska Highway. Between the darkness, rockfall exposure, and scale of the terrain, Wales told Outside that a traditional rope rescue or helicopter evacuation would have been especially difficult. “Both of those options being dangerous and challenging, the managers called up our drone team with a bit of an idea,” Wales said. “We theorized that we could deliver a pilot line to the person stranded on the wall.” The stranded person had been climbing with two other people, who were able to safely scale down the wall. Wales and five other rescuers met them and established communication with the cliffed-out climber, putting a plan in place. “When you’re doing a drone operation, it’s really important to discuss the risks when you have the opportunity to do so,” Wales said. “Through our communication, we were able to ask the climber if he was confident to come down, and also what he needed to come down.” For the first flight, rescuers tethered a pilot line to the drone and flew it up to the climber. Once he had a hold of the line, responders on the ground tied a jacket and headlamp to it, which he then pulled up to himself. He used the gear to stay warm and light the rock. Based on the climber’s information, Wales and his team then used the drone to measure the distance to the ground with lasers and a rangefinder. They then brought in a larger drone with a light, which hovered to spotlight the cliffed-out climber. Rescuers tied a 300-foot pilot line from the smaller drone to a climbing rope, and flew the device to the climber. The rope was a thin-gauge but high-strength Dyneema line, which the team spooled out between a ground operator and the drone. According to Wales, the climber “captured the rope out of the air.” He then tied the line to his climbing harness and an anchor, and rappelled down to safety. Flying drones are becoming common in search and rescue teams worldwide. In recent years, lifesaving officials have used them to spot lost hikers, drop food and water, and take aerial images of huge swaths of backcountry. The Squamish incident shows that drones can also deliver climbing gear to someone in a highly precarious position. “This rescue is a great representation of flight skills, training, management, and practice,” Wales said. “It’s a pretty big win for us. There was a lot of cheering from the ground crew. It was an awesome demonstration of what a lot of effort, training, and facilitation can culminate in.”

item.title: ‘High Ground’ Documentary Uncovers the True Story of the 1977 Yosemite Weed Plane Crash
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.00
(Photo: Ron Lykins) You would think a movie about a plane crash with three tons of illegal Mexican weed onboard, two fatalities, a run-in with the Drug Enforcement Agency, and a classic climbers versus park rangers clash would be filled with bad guys. A lot of bad guys. But as it turns out, it is possible to make a feel-good movie about the “legend of dope lake.” Aside from the death of two pilots, could the drug plane crash of 1976 actually have had a positive ripple effect through Yosemite Valley? At a time when we’re all sorely in need of feel-good stories, the new documentary High Ground—the first full-length film about this storied incident—delivers a dose of optimism. How can the tale of a Howard 500 aircraft with three tons (over 6,000 pounds) of weed on board crashing into Lower Merced Pass Lake be uplifting? For that answer, we asked one of the climbers who scored a bale of Mexican weed for himself. Produced by British film production company Dash Pictures, the one-and-a-half-hour doc sheds ample new light on the legend through in-depth interviews with park rangers, a widow of one of the pilots, a U.S. customs agent, the former head of Yosemite Search and Rescue, and climbers who fetched bales of wet marijuana from the lake over the course of a few months. One of those climbers, Ken Yager, founded and now leads the Yosemite Climbing Association, which runs a small museum in the park. Today, the museum displays seven pieces of airplane debris from the crash. For Yager and several other climbers interviewed in High Ground, this is the first time they’ve come public with their stories from the drug rush of 1997 (the plane crashed on December 8, 1976, but wasn’t discovered until January 27, 1977). “People have talked about doing this story for a long time,” Yager told Climbing, adding that several production companies have inquired with him about filming documentaries. How did a bunch of non-climbing Brits end up being the first to produce a feature-length film on the subject? In short, Leo Houlding. Director Daniel Sharp met the pro climber a decade ago through a mutual friend. When Sharp moved to California in 2016, Houlding relayed the tale. The first person Sharp met in Yosemite was climbing photographer Dean Fidelman, who shared his account of what went down decades ago. Fidelman’s report led to more people and more sides of the story, ultimately convincing Sharp that a proper documentary was in order. Sharp calls Yager “the single most key” person when it came to finding other sources and getting “a sense for the project.” Most climbers and rangers involved, including Yager, had decided that 50 years was enough time passed to come out of the woodwork. Only two sources were still unwilling to talk, according to Sharp. “We did a lot of work to reassure people the statute has long since passed,” he told Climbing. One person declined involvement because they were still employed with the park. “We also did a lot of work to reassure people from all sides that we wouldn’t make them look silly, that we wanted to tell a balanced and true story, and that we deal with what’s fact, what’s rumor and what’s memory, and how that changes over time.” Some of the interviewees have died since filming. Dale Bard, a talented climber who established the Sea of Dreams climbing route on El Capitan, passed away on October 1, 2025. (You can read a posthumous letter to him from a former climbing partner here.) Ranger Rick Smith died in July. “We wanted to capture this generation of Yosemite climbers and rangers while they could still tell the story themselves, contradictions and all,” Sharp said. Another less-discussed fatality related to the Yosemite plane crash incident (besides the pilots) is the climber Jack Dorn—a thread that High Ground explores, but doesn’t resolve. Dorn allegedly became enmeshed in a dark web of contacts found in the pilot’s recovered “black book.” Soon after, he died in a fall from a hiking trail at night. But some, including Bard, speculated that he may have been pushed. We sat down with Yager to find out why he finally felt ready to come forward with his account. He also revealed whether that frozen plane weed was any good, and how he thinks the plane crash inadvertently may have shaped Yosemite climbing history. CLIMBING: Why did you choose to remain quiet about your participation in the Yosemite plane crash incident until now? Ken Yager: I’ve talked about it before, but always with an alias. The first time I talked about it publicly, I did an interview with Men’s Journal and it’s called “The Legend of Dope Lake.” My alias was Chuck Strader; I didn’t make it up, they made it up. I didn’t talk about it before using my name for a couple reasons: One, I had a young daughter who wasn’t 18 yet. In case there was any blowback or repercussions, I didn’t want to embarrass her. The other reason was that I was still pushing hard to get a permitted space in the park for the museum. What made you decide to come forward as a source after all these years? First of all, I’ve done everything I wanted to do. I got the park partnership and the museum. I started all these things that have been big dreams of mine for 35 years or more. Then I realized something two years ago, when I opened the museum. The National Park Service (NPS) interpretive teams and law enforcement came down and got tours. The thing they were most interested in was seeing the airplane parts. They’re buying airplane shirts. I said, “You used to chase us for the silliest little things. Were you guys bored or what?” They pretty much said, Oh yeah, we were bored and you were a challenge. It was like a game for them. Now I’m friends with them—sort of. I mean we don’t hang out or anything. Enough time has passed that we can talk about it and chuckle about it and go, Wow, times have really changed. How do you feel about the film, now that it’s premiered? I really like everything about it—how Daniel with Dash Productions is releasing it, how he’s respectful to everyone. It’s Daniel’s 33rd documentary and he said this is the one he’s most excited about. An American director would have had an antagonist. To me, it was a really relatable human story about everyone involved. Nobody looks bad. The plane crashed three days after I showed up in the valley. It’s like it crashed just for me. The whole thing is bizarre, but it helped a lot of people. In your perspective, is that sentiment that the film portrays—no antagonists—accurate? With the park service, the thing fell in their lap and they did the best they could. It’s more just a set of circumstances where everyone was trying to do their thing. For the climbing community, they couldn’t resist. Some people did it for the money, some did it for the thrill. And some did it just to get weed because it was highly illegal back then in every state, let alone on federal property. It was a whole different world back then. It’s still illegal federally in the park. It was a crazy time and nobody knew what to do. We were all in over our heads. I had just turned 18 and I would be tried as an adult. I just wanted some weed. The turn of events just got more and more serious. I lucked out and realized I never wanted to be involved in that business. I just really like the fact that [Sharp] didn’t make anybody bad. Nobody wanted it to escalate. What did you buy with your plane weed profits? How much cash did you walk away with? Some of the weed, I didn’t know what to do with. I gave it to a friend of mine from high school who did. I did buy a $500 Volkswagen. Then I traded a bunch for all the climbing gear I needed that I didn’t have. I used it to climb El Cap. I climbed El Cap four times that year with hip belays and no cams. Those were the days. Just stoppers, hexes, and pitons—it’s a trip. I did ascents of Tangerine Trip and Zodiac. I was the first nobody to do them. They became trade routes. If that hippie can do them, then we can do them. A year or two later, they got done all the time. Was the weed any good? It’s hard to imagine the marijuana being in decent condition after soaking in a lake filled with plane debris and dead bodies—and covered in jet fuel. I remember well. First of all, as I mentioned, weed was highly illegal back then. Most American weed was horrible. Back then, the best weed were Thai sticks and stuff from Mexico—Acupulco Gold, Panama Red, or whatever. They were all high-end, south-of-border pots. The bags were burlap sacks with three layers of plastic around them that of course didn’t work. They all had a label on them. The one I found was 27 kilos (2.2 pounds) before it got wet. The one I had was Double A Grade Mexican (it goes up to triple grade). It dried out and it was still very, very potent. Some of the bales were worse than others. There were bales really close to where the fuel puddle was under the ice. If you peeled off an inch or two out of the bales, the center of the bales were damn good. Just wet. For us, it was a great thing. A little smell of airplane fuel, but most of it evaporated off. The film portrays the lake as quite a scene, by turns spooky, weird, fun, and legitimately dangerous. What was the vibe like at the lake in your experience? I was scared shitless. When I went up there, I got in and out in 22 hours. My mom and her husband were visiting with my stepbrothers and sisters. I was supposed to be spending time with them. So I told them I was going to be climbing at Mount Starr King. My brothers and sisters all knew what was going on. As you’re going up to the lake, wading through icy rivers, you arrive soaking wet. I remember it being windy, cold. You could see planes flying over, not down low, but you’re thinking they’re just watching you up there. I was super paranoid. When I walked up on the shore, you could see insulation, fuel lines, metal wrapped around the trees. And you could smell the oil and hydraulics and fuel, too. It’s super spooky. You know there’s death there. Are there any notable milestones in climbing history that you would correlate with the plane crash? I would say a lot of people did. People did climbing trips to Colorado, went up in the Cirque of the Unclimbables, or they went to Europe. A lot of people went on to climb in other areas they might not have been able to make it to because it involved plane fare. As far as big climbs since then, certainly people stayed around and did first ascents or lots of other climbs, Mike Corbett being one of them. El Cap routes—hard El Cap routes. Sea of Dreams got done the following year. Around that time was Bill Price’s 5.13—a lot of hard free climbing happened then. People were doing some really good climbs at that time, but whether it was because of the airplane I can’t really say. I’m sure it influenced it. A lot of people benefitted from it. People were very generous with it. It’s a little different than nowadays. My God, I can still remember the taste of it. What does the Yosemite Climbing Museum have as far as exhibits related to the plane crash? I have seven pieces of the airplane wreckage. The biggest you can see at the very end of the credits in [the documentary] Valley Uprising—that’s me holding a piece of the fuselage. It could be part of the wing, I have no idea. It’s a sheet of aluminum that’s maybe three feet by five feet. I’ve got a hydraulic pump, some pieces of fuel line. Piece of fuselage or wing. We also sell airplane t-shirts. What is your theory about what happened to Dorn on the Yosemite Falls Trail? I don’t think he was pushed. It just seems a little far-fetched. It was speculation. The way I understand it is that my friend Sean Plunkett actually had the book. He was up there when [Dorn] got the money. My girlfriend at the time worked at the bank. I knew there were soaking wet bills they brought to the bank to exchange. Everywhere I turned, I was involved in it. Everyone was involved. Even if they didn’t go up there, they had friends that did. As the unofficial historian of Yosemite climbing history, how do you view this incident? I think it’s the crowning piece of history as far as the seventies go—it was a very tumultuous time. It started in 1970 with the riots. That scared the park service. Shortly after, they created the LEO [Law Enforcement Officer] arm of the park service—in other words, people carrying guns. The people who had the sit-in at the meadow that caused the riots all looked like the climbers of the seventies—or we all looked like them. We had long hair, we had beards, we’re up there climbing with very little money. The last thing we’re going to do is go get a haircut or buy a razor. I’ve never even owned a comb. There was prejudice there. We’d get harassed. There wasn’t really anything going on. We were the eyesore of the community and looked like bums. Also the law enforcement and park service and Curry Company people, a lot of them didn’t like us because quite honestly they weren’t really fit. Climbers always had girlfriends and a cabin to stay in during the winter. There was a lot of jealousy there. Climbers weren’t having to work and they were. Climbers were having fun and all the female employees seemed to really like them and they didn’t like that. I kind of get it. The other thing I’ll say is that the park service harassing the climbing community and the climbing community pushing back became this kind of cold or invisible war. When I first moved up there, I was a little kid but I learned pretty quickly to stay away from that guy, listen for the radio, and so on. There were undercover people up there to listen in on you—it’s really weird. How did the dope plane crash change that dynamic? In some ways, it created a little bit of a truce and was kind of the turning point to eventually getting along. First of all, we didn’t want anyone to know we went up there. We were scared. Number two: If I was an NPS person investigating that, I’d feel like I screwed up. I wouldn’t want that story to get out either. We were all like: Let’s pretend this didn’t happen and go back to where we were. What really turned it around was the Facelift [a volunteer cleaning event] and the movies lately and a lot more climbers working for the park service and the concessionaire. But it was the culmination of that antagonist relationship between the park service and the climbing community. It took many, many years before it got to where it is now, but I think it was the start of it. Was the Yosemite Facelift inspired in any way by the mess left by the crash? I’ve never been afraid to clean stuff up. I lived off of canning too for a while. A nickel a can back then with everyone not recycling was so easy—then you could go out for dinner and get a beer. I made up to $80 one day. Back then, that was a lot of money. I started [Facelift] because I was a climbing guide and one of my jobs was to talk about Leave No Trace principles. Sort of hard when you’re tip-toeing on the trail and behind every rock there’s a bunch of toilet paper and cigarette butts. I just felt like I was being hypocritical by ignoring it. I’d get so mad, but I’m not going to pick up toilet paper and put it in my climbing pack. I thought: I can be mad about it for the rest of my life, or I can turn it around and do something about it. Interview was edited for space and clarity. High Ground premiered at the Yosemite Cinema in Oakhurst, California, on September 5. It will be playing again during the weekend of Yosemite Facelift—an event established and spearheaded by Yager through the YCA—from September 23-27. The documentary will also screen at the San Diego Film Festival on October 16 and 17. Dash Pictures expects small theatrical releases, as well as additional film festival screenings in the next few months, but can’t announce details yet. It will likely be available to stream or rent online in early 2027. Follow @highgroundmovie for updates.

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape.” Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.85
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management (BLM) order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from a BLM order this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to reclassify livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species of its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led American Prairie to cancel its public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here, and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: 5 Yoga-Inspired Foot and Ankle Exercises to Help You Move Better Outdoors
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.32
(Photo: Canva) Bad news: your feet are likely chronically compromised. When it comes to stretching and strengthening, the feet are easily one of the most overlooked parts of the body, despite the fact that you rely on them for literally each step you take. Runners and other outdoor athletes are especially vulnerable to foot issues. “The foot is the body’s primary interface with the ground,” says Devon Crahan, yoga teacher and owner of Intentional Yoga, a hot yoga studio based in Michigan. According to Crahan, research continues to demonstrate the influence of the foot on movement quality throughout the body. Over time, the dozens of intricate muscles, tendons, and ligaments in your feet naturally weaken and atrophy. Without that structural support, your inner arches start to flatten, making your ankles roll inward. As a result, it’s natural to subconsciously dump more of your weight into your knees and ankles. Eventually, this repetitive strain can compound and become a painful issue throughout your body. Crahan explains that when you rebuild the structural strength in your feet, your knees and hips function more efficiently since the foundation beneath them is better able to absorb and transmit force. It’s possible to improve the mechanics of your feet and ankles with simple stretching and strengthening exercises. An unexpected benefit of bringing more awareness to the feet is paying attention to how you land on them. “I’ll often see practitioners lean too much weight forward into the front toes, which presents itself as pinched-up, or overflexing,” Crahan says, explaining that this can cause cramping. “Learn to lean your weight back a bit, using the front toes strictly for fine-tuning your balance. When practiced consistently, even a simple 5-minute foot yoga routine can help protect your feet, your body mechanics, and your balance in everyday life and on the trails. Regularly stretching and strengthening your feet not only brings more steadiness to your everyday life, but also helps you find more stability on your mat during a yoga class or on the trails. When balancing on the balls of your feet in a squat, you transfer the entire weight of the body onto the arches and toes, which activates the stabilizing muscles to build strength. Focus on: The intense activation in your toes and arches. Lift your heels as high as you can rather than letting them hover. Keep your spine straight and keep your chest from rounding forward as you steady your balance. Continue to breathe. An increasingly common pose in yoga classes, Toe Squat is a variation on Thunderbolt Pose (Vajrasana) that stretches the plantar fascia, the muscle that runs along the bottom of your feet, and strengthens the stabilizing muscles of the toes and ankles. Focus on: The intense opening along the bottoms of your feet. Send your awareness into the center of the tightness, focusing on slow, steady breaths and extended exhalations. This dynamic variation of a simple standing pose strengthens the calves and trains the ankles to stay centered and steady under pressure. This counteracts the tendency to roll the ankles slightly inward, which can compromise knee alignment. Focus on: The alignment of your ankles and the shifting distribution of weight. Notice if your weight spills outward toward your pinky toes and actively press down through the balls of your big toes to keep your weight more centered toward the midline of your body. In yogic tradition, pada bandha (foot lock) is the intentional act of rooting down through the four major corners of the foot (the ball of the big toe, the ball of the little toe, the inner heel, and the outer heel) while actively lifting the inner arches upward like a dome. This practice teaches you to track the exact boundaries of your feet while training you to evenly distribute your weight as you stand. Focus on: The physical sensation in your feet. Feel your arches lift away from the floor as the edges of your feet, heels, and toes press into the mat as if they were glued down. Think of it as an energetic bridge that draws energy up from the ground through your feet. Slowing down and practicing heel-to-toe walks help you consciously track where you place most of your weight. In turn, this can help you rewire any subconscious walking habits that could lead to chronic foot strain. Focus on: The urge to rush. Take your time. Also note the precise micro-moments of skin contact with the floor. Draw your mind entirely into the rolling sensation of your weight transferring from heel to toe. Over time, those daily five-minute foot exercises and foot stretches will build a resilient, lasting capacity of your feet to carry you gracefully, on the mat and on the trails. item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston said. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW teams have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without breaks. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the five-year average, and euthanization is up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as he spoke on the phone with Backpacker. “It’s been a busy year,” he said. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he said: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston pointed to the record-low snowpack that caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston said, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he said. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explained. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston pointed out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also said that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze black bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston said. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.81
‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food. The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended. “Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home. Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses. Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work. Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli. Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from. At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed. At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations. But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills. Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce. At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930. Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs. At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.” In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie. Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses. Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb. It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious. It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. item.title: Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west Sweden
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.94
I wasn’t exactly in “Sunday best”, but I had made some effort. Well, I’d changed my underwear for the first time in a couple of days and given myself a baby-wipe bath. Still, as we filed into the chapel at Alkavare, I felt more a member of an expedition than a congregation. We sat on the low wooden benches, waterproof jackets rustling and leather walking boots stamping on the flagstone floor to keep warm. Fortunately, the priest, Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen, appeared to be a “man of the Gore-Tex”, as well as a man of the cloth, as he unzipped his own black rain jacket to reveal his dog collar. As the service began, the Arctic wind whipped through cracks in the dry stone walls, insulated only with reindeer hair, and candles flickered in their brass sconces. I had hiked to Alkavare following the Präststigen, or “Priests’ trail”, a 37-mile (60km) route from Kvikkjokk that could stake a claim as Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route, and certainly one of its most beautiful. The Präststigen follows the path that priests would once have taken to the chapel, built in 1788, to perform a service each summer, and today, on the last weekend in July, intrepid hikers and perseverant pilgrims can attend that same service. Alkavare sits on the western border of Sweden’s Sarek national park, home to many of the country’s highest mountains and steepest valleys, yet with no campsites or tourist huts and only scant sections of the more famous Kungsleden trail. There are no other marked paths and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventure. It was described by famed Swedish diplomat Dag Hammarskjöld in 1926 as vår sista stora vildmark – “our last great wilderness”. “I hate it when people use the term ‘wilderness’,” Christian Heimrot from Laponia Adventures, a local guiding operator, told me, as I joined him on the research exhibition for a new Präststigen group trip launching next year. “This is a living landscape, people have lived, worked and shaped this land for thousands of years.” Indeed, Sarek national park, (as part of the wider Laponia region), was recognised as a Unsesco World Heritage Site in 1996 for both its cultural and natural value. The Sami, Europe’s last Indigenous population, have braided themselves into these landscapes as tightly and beautifully as the thread of pewter in their traditional handicrafts. The Sami word for the Laponia area is Sápmi, the same word they use to refer to themselves, highlighting the indelible link between people and their environment. Sarek sits on the Sami’s traditional reindeer herding grounds. While they might now use motorcycles and snowmobiles to follow and herd the reindeer, their knowledge of and kinship with this landscape remains undimmed. So, not wilderness, then, but certainly wild. To even reach the start of the Präststigen, I had crossed the Arctic Circle on the road north from Luleå, met with Christian at his warehouse in Jokkmokk (home to the famous Sami winter markets each February) to load up our rucksacks for the six-night trip, and journeyed an hour farther west to the town of Kvikkjokk. From there the trailhead was a short boat ride across Sakkat lake. The first section of the trail climbed steeply, switchbacks tightly coiled in birch woodland; wild blueberries and cloudberries littered the path. Eventually we left the woodland and reached the ridge for our first proper view of Sarek. Away to the north was the cloud-covered summit of Bårddetjåhkkå, where in 1911 Swedish geologist Axel Hamberg built an observatory to conduct meteorological and glacial studies. We slept soundly, as we eased into the rhythms of wild camping – water collected from a gin-clear lake, a hearty supper of reindeer stew, and an eye mask to keep out the midnight sun. The next day we hiked deeper into Sarek via the Vállevágge, the skies the blue of the Swedish flag, the silence only disrupted by the occasional breath of wind. We were following the guidebook Priest’s Path by Hans Fowelin (currently only published in Swedish), and while there was no marked trail, Fowelin had plotted a path of cairns we were supposedly to follow. While some were solidly built square towers, most were little more than one rock propped up against another, mere whispers of waymarkers in a landscape of scree and moraine. Alongside the familiar buttercups and heather there were bright blue blossoms of mountain gentian, red ptarmigan berries and otherworldly looking wild angelica, a source of vitamin C for the Sami. Sarek was visited by botanist Carl Linnaeus during his epic expedition through northern Sweden in 1732, and the first part of the Priest’s trail is sometimes referred to as Linnaeus’s trail. On our fourth day of hiking Alkavare chapel appeared on a bluff above the glacial blue waters of Alggajavvre lake, surrounded by high peaks and valleys. It was utterly beautiful. I had a grin on my wind-burnt face for most of the day, one that even wading across rivers (a common feature of hiking in Sarek), shin-high in glacial meltwater, failed to dim. After rowing across the Miellätno river, using one of the rowing boats left on each bank by the park rangers, we climbed up to the chapel late on Saturday evening where Jacobsen greeted us with a beaming smile. Over tea, he told us he had been dropped off by helicopter at Alkavare with his family on Friday morning and this was his first time leading the service here. Others in the diocese no longer volunteered. “It is physical, hard work and the days are long,” he said, before heading off to re-tar the chapel’s roof and fix one of the rowing boats that had come loose and floated away down the river – returned, later, swinging beneath a helicopter. Sunday mass began promptly at 11am the following morning for our small band of pilgrims (we numbered 11 in total, including the priest). The altar had a simple wooden cross and cloths on loan from the church in Jokkmokk. They were in the poster paint palate of traditional Sami clothing and a reminder that it was for the Sami that the chapel had been originally built – not an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation and eradication of their shamanistic beliefs in the 18th century. After the service we sat outside for coffee and pastries, before beginning our hike home. Christian was keen that we hiked via Sweden’s point of inaccessibility or otillgänglighetspunkten, just over the border from Sarek in the Padjelanta national park. This is the country’s point furthest from any road or town, about 31 miles (50km) in fact, and is often cited as western Europe’s remotest too. Marked with no cairn or monument, just a circle of quartz stones and a trio of reindeer antlers, it felt no more or less remote than most of the previous week’s hiking. And I was struck that what made Sarek and the Präststigen special wasn’t just the scenery, as beautiful as it was, it was the people – the Sami, Hamberg and Linneaus, and the motley congregation we’d briefly joined, and it was a route firmly deserving of more visitors. “I told you,” Christian said, grinning, “It isn’t a wilderness.” The trip was provided by Laponia Adventures, which will lead a guided, small-group trip along the Priest’s Path to Alkavare in July 2027, and offers equipment rental and advice for independent hikers. item.title: 7 reasons you might want the Amex Business Platinum instead of the Amex Platinum
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.03
7 reasons you might want the Amex Business Platinum instead of the Amex Platinum Editor's Note Thanks to its stellar portfolio of perks and all the incredible uses there are for American Express Membership Rewards points, we often focus on the American Express Platinum Card®. Some folks even forget that the card has a counterpart, The Business Platinum Card® from American Express, that offers many of the same benefits as the personal card, along with some that make it a great choice for small-business owners. Using a business card like the Amex Business Platinum for work-related purchases can help you separate your personal and business expenses so your end-of-year accounting is a bit easier, too, which is a factor in its favor. Here's a quick look at both cards side by side and a helpful list of reasons why the Amex Business Platinum might actually be a better choice for some folks. Related: Is the Amex Business Platinum worth the annual fee? Comparing the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum Let's start with a quick snapshot of both cards and their benefits. | | Amex Platinum | Amex Business Platinum | |---|---|---| | Welcome offer | Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. | Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 300,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. | | Annual fee | | | | Earning rates | | | | Unique benefits | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | As you can see, each card offers a robust slate of benefits specific to its own cardmembers. But the two cards also have a menu of similar perks to be aware of, which will help you with your decision about which card to get. Related: 9 things to do when you get the Amex Business Platinum Card Perks offered by both cards Here are the benefits that both the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum cards offer — meaning you will be able to take advantage of these no matter which card you opt for (enrollment is required for select benefits): - Up to $600 statement credit each calendar year (up to $300 biannually) on prepaid bookings at Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection properties made through Amex Travel (minimum two-night stay requirement for The Hotel Collection) - An airline fee statement credit of up to $200 per calendar year on charges with the eligible U.S. airline you select - Get $120 as a statement credit for a Global Entry application fee or a statement credit of up to $85 for TSA PreCheck once every four years - Receive a statement credit per calendar year to reimburse your annual Clear+ membership fee (up to $219 per calendar year; subject to auto-renewal). - Eligible cardmembers can access the American Express Global Lounge Collection, which includes Centurion Lounges, Priority Pass™ lounges, Delta Sky Clubs (limited to 10 annual visits; when flying on a same-day Delta flight; except basic economy flights; spend $75,000 in a calendar year to unlock unlimited flights), Aspire lounges, Escape lounges, Plaza Premium lounges and Lufthansa lounges - Complimentary car elite rental status with Hertz President's Circle, Avis Preferred Plus and National Emerald Club Executive - Complimentary Gold elite status with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, plus Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World - No foreign transaction fees (see rates and fees for the Amex Platinum and rates and fees for the Amex Business Platinum) - Benefit from various travel protections and purchase protections Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum Reasons to choose the Amex Business Platinum over the Amex Platinum Now that you have a full rundown of benefits to refer to, here are some key reasons and spending habits that might lead you to choose the Business Platinum Card instead of the Amex Platinum. 1. You have or already had the personal Amex Platinum If you currently carry the personal Amex Platinum Card, or even if you previously had it but no longer do, you might not be eligible to earn its welcome offer. That's because, like many other issuers, American Express has restricted who is eligible for the welcome bonuses on its cards. So, if you already have, or previously had, the Amex Platinum, you might be blocked from taking advantage of its current welcome offer. If you want the card's benefits and the chance to earn hundreds of thousands of additional Membership Rewards points, however, you might opt for the Business Platinum instead, since currently or previously carrying the personal Amex Platinum should not preclude you from being eligible for the Business Platinum's welcome bonus. Related: 10 things to do when you get the Amex Platinum 2. You spend enough to earn the Amex Business Platinum's higher welcome offer The Business Platinum welcome offer requires some strategic spending, as the requirement is $20,000 in purchases within the first three months of card membership. That's a considerable sum, but it's not outside the usual operating budget of some small businesses. By contrast, the Platinum currently has a lower spending requirement of $12,000 within the first six months of card membership to earn its welcome offer. And note: You have double the time of the business version to reach it. The personal card's terms might work better for your spending habits. However, the fact that you can potentially earn nearly twice as many points with the Business Platinum is a worthwhile consideration (not everyone will be targeted for the same welcome offers). 3. You spend a lot on flights and hotels, specifically The two cards have very similar earning structures when it comes to travel, with two subtle but significant differences. The personal card earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked through Amex Travel and directly with airlines on up to $500,000 in purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent after that. The Business Platinum earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked through Amex Travel (not directly with airlines) with no spending cap. Both cards earn 5 points per dollar spent on prepaid hotel bookings with Amex Travel. If you tend to book flights directly with airlines, the personal card might be a better choice. However, if you use Amex Travel for a lot of your travel plans — or if you have that option — then you won't miss out by charging your reservations to the Business Platinum. Plus, if you book a lot of flights, or more than $500,000 worth per year, specifically, with your card, then you're definitely better off with the business card since its bonus-qualifying spending isn't capped at that amount. Just remember that the Amex Business Platinum only earns bonus points on flights booked through Amex Travel, unless the charge is for $5,000 or more (subject to a spending cap). Related: The best credit cards for paying taxes and fees on award tickets 4. You can maximize the Amex Business Platinum's large-transaction and business category bonuses If you tend to make a lot of high-dollar purchases or spend a lot in certain categories, then the Business Platinum's earning structure can really set you ahead. The card accrues points at the following rates. - 2 points per dollar spent on purchases of $5,000 or more - 2 points per dollar spent on U.S. purchases from construction material and hardware suppliers, electronic goods retailers, shipping providers, and software and cloud system providers There is a combined $2 million spending cap per calendar year (then 1 point per dollar spent). If these are the types of business purchases you tend to make — or if you regularly use your card for transactions of more than $5,000 — then the Business Platinum blows the personal version's earning rates out of the water. You might also find creative ways to leverage these bonuses on one-off purchases. Related: The top 7 credit cards to maximize large purchases 5. You use Amex Pay with Points for premium travel One major way the two cards diverge is that the Business Platinum Card offers cardmembers a bonus 35% of the points back they redeem through Amex's Pay with Points feature, while the personal version does not. There are a few stipulations, though. First, you only receive the 35% points bonus on flights booked through Amex Travel on the same qualifying airline you designate for the up to $200 per calendar year airline fee statement credit. The good news is, the ticket can be in any cabin class, not just a premium one. Second, you can only receive up to 1 million points back per year. To max that out, you'd have to be redeeming nearly 2.9 million Amex points, though, so this cap shouldn't impact most people. Even if you seldom redeem Membership Rewards points this way, this one benefit can save you tens of thousands of points on a single ticket. 6. You prefer the business card's statement credits The personal and business versions each offer many annual statement credits. Some are the same, but many are unique to each card. The personal card offers quite a few lifestyle statement credits. But if those aren't things you actually use normally, why bother trying to track them while juggling the card's steep annual fee? The Business Platinum offers thousands of dollars in annual statement credits with popular business-related merchants. (Enrollment is required for select benefits; select benefits are subject to auto-renewal.) Plus, with the Business Platinum, you'll earn up to $1,200 in Amex Travel flight statement credits and up to $2,400 in One AP statement credits (valid from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31 of the calendar year after meeting the requirement), after spending $250,000 or more on eligible purchases in a calendar year. While this is a substantial spending requirement, if you can meet it through your regular spending activity, the Business Platinum could be a better option. That said, these benefits aren't substantial enough to make it worth going out of your way to spend that much on the Business Platinum. Related: Who should (and shouldn't) get the Amex Business Platinum? 7. You are interested in adding employee cards The personal Amex Platinum Card allows you to add up to 10 active authorized users. You can either add them as additional Platinum Card holders at a cost of $195 per card per year (see rates and fees) with some of the card's travel benefits, including lounge access, or as Companion Card holders with no annual fee (see rates and fees) and very limited benefits. By contrast, the Business Platinum allows you to add up to 99 additional Employee Cards. Full Business Platinum additional cards with some of the same benefits afforded to the primary cardmember carry a $400 annual fee each (see rates and fees). Employee Expense cards have no annual fee (see rates and fees). All card activity can be tracked through Amex. For business owners who need to track employee spending (and who would like to earn points for themselves on all that spending), the Business Platinum lets you have many more cards under your umbrella and allows you to track them easily. Bottom line Both the Amex Platinum and the Business Platinum are excellent rewards cards with a variety of benefits from which members can reap tremendous value. Consider which card best matches your financial habits and needs, and which card's other perks you're most likely to leverage year after year. And after all that, you might even want to consider carrying both the personal and business Amex Platinum cards since there are plenty of ways the two cards don't overlap. To learn more, check out our full reviews of the Amex Platinum and Amex Business Platinum. item.title: Sports travel is having its 'Eras Tour' moment. Airlines have noticed
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.72
Sports travel is having its 'Eras Tour' moment. Airlines have noticed Next month, the reigning national champion Indiana University Hoosiers head to Lincoln, Nebraska, for a college football showdown against the University of Nebraska Cornhuskers. United Airlines is planning to help with the fan frenzy. The carrier plans to offer a rare flight between Indianapolis and Lincoln on game weekend. Normally, it wouldn't connect those two cities with nonstop service. There are more flights like that one, too. That same week, United will also offer unusual nonstop service between Eugene, Oregon, and Columbus, Ohio, catering to a high-stakes University of Oregon-Ohio State University matchup. Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines has added a full slate of flights this fall, specifically to carry fans to away games. And later this month, American Airlines will go bigger and farther: When the Dallas Cowboys head to Brazil for an NFL game, American will offer a special flight from Dallas to Rio de Janeiro on one of its large Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Everywhere you look right now, airlines are leaning into sports. For good reason, too. "The local market in sports is so popular right now, and so much money is being spent," Joe Esposito, chief commercial officer at Delta Air Lines, said last month when speaking on a panel in Texas. "No matter where you look in this country — whether it's college, pro, WNBA — everything is packed," he added. "It's an insatiable business." Sports travel is booming In 2025, fans spent $51.1 billion traveling to spectator sporting events, according to the Sports Events and Tourism Association. And keep in mind that was before fans flooded major U.S. cities this summer for the FIFA World Cup. In Austin, one out of every six hotel room nights is now owed to sports-related travel, tourism leaders say. "It drives summer. It drives weekend[s]," Tom Noonan, CEO of Visit Austin, said last month. "It's a big part of Austin's future." It's about how fans are traveling Of course, fans following their teams around the country is nothing new. Rose Gray, a Wisconsin-based travel adviser, has helped Green Bay Packers fans book trips to away games for more than 40 years. What has changed, she said, is how fans are choosing to travel. Gone are the days of scoring cheap tickets, staying in budget motels and tailgating to beat traffic. Now, fans are asking Gray to send them to Formula One races in Monaco with prime seats and meet and greets with their favorite drivers. "They may say, 'I don't want to just stay in some Motel Six an hour away from the Masters," Gray, of Fox World Travel, said. "They're looking for an experience. It's not just a game. It's talking to the locals. Learning about the local cuisine. Being as close as possible." It's a cultural phenomenon cut from the same cloth as the all-in approach Taylor Swift fans took while booking trips to The Eras Tour in 2023 and 2024: expensive hotels, luxe dinners and high-end experiences. In the face of stubborn inflation and higher borrowing costs, it might be the latest sign that consumers are refusing to sacrifice travel even as they face difficult spending decisions. "I don't think the splurge is necessarily people that are all really wealthy," Wendy Zajack, adjunct professor who studies consumer behavior at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said. "I think people are willing to save for a big trip or a big moment," Zajack added. "And when they do it, they're going to do it all in." Airlines bet big on the big game Airlines have taken notice. Southwest is planning unique nonstop service between Oklahoma City and Jacksonville when Oklahoma State plays the University of Florida in November. The weekend before Thanksgiving, there's a flight between Columbus and Omaha when Ohio State plays Nebraska. To be fair, these football-focused flights aren't actually new. United has been strategically adding unique routes to college football games for nearly a decade. But in recent years, the Chicago-based carrier has doubled down on finding opportunities to add one-off routes, even ones that don't touch its major hubs. A prime example is the flight between Birmingham, Alabama, and Baton Rouge, Louisiana, which it added for the Nov. 7 Alabama-LSU matchup. "We've developed a much deeper understanding of where fans want to go and how they prefer to travel," Michael Weeks, United's managing director of domestic schedule development, told TPG. "That experience," he said, "has helped us become more strategic in identifying the right games, matching capacity to demand, and creating schedules that work well for customers." More than a game The deep link between sports and travel goes well beyond Saturday college football games, too — especially as leagues launch games to more alluring destinations. The NFL is planning its biggest international tour in 2026, following this past week's first-ever game in Australia. Next summer, the MLB plans to host another game on the Iowa farm that was once the set of the film "Field of Dreams." Meanwhile, ticket sales are already underway for one of the biggest draws of all: the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. At a time when so much in life now happens on a screen, traveling to these "in-real-life" games increasingly feels like a splurge worth planning a larger trip around, according to Zajack. "I think in our world right now we are really craving unique time-bound events," she said. "I don't see an end to it right now." TPG's tips for booking If you're planning to book a trip to see your favorite team, it helps to be an eagle-eyed schedule-watcher. Begin searching flights and hotels as soon as your team's schedule drops. If you're hoping to use points, the best award deals are sometimes available 11 months or more in advance. Just be sure to book reservations you can change if the price later drops or if your plans change. Consider protecting your trip with a travel insurance plan that covers major events like sports games or concerts. And, when possible, add another layer of protection by purchasing your travel with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance. Because flight prices typically surge around major events, plan to land a few days early and leave a couple of days after the final whistle. This can add peace of mind if you get delayed and help you avoid high-demand ticket prices. Plus, you'll get to experience the destination more fully. Finally, be strategic when using points and miles. While award bookings can reduce your out-of-pocket expenses on flights and hotels, consult our valuations to ensure you're not handing too many hard-earned points over at once. Related reading:
